speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think this may be the appropriate time to mention the matter because, in the ordinary course of events if Your Honour were giving a ruling, it would be at this time that you would give it. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext: Order. May I inform the Leader of the Opposition that that matter cannot be taken up at this time. The order of the house to go into committee of supply and the debate on the amendment and the amendment to the amendment will be resumed when it is necessary for the Speaker again to put the motion to go into supply. That will be perhaps on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. Today, however, that debate will not be resumed. In any event, this would not be the time to discuss the observations I made last night in connection with the amendment. That discussion will have to take place when the order is read for resuming the adjourned debate on the motion to go into supply and on the amendment and the amendment to the amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was about to point out that under rulings that have been made the fact that this matter remains in a state of suspense conceivably could have some effect on the scope of the debate under the Department of Trade and Commerce which, we have been informed, is to be the first department called today. I was merely suggesting the possibility that if Your Honour had reached a decision, that decision conceivably could have some bearing on the breadth of the remarks that could be made on the first item of the Department of Trade and Commerce. If Your Honour feels that that matter should stand, then it would be necessary for those who speak to guide themselves accordingly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, it is not a matter of the Speaker feeling that it should stand; it is because I cannot deal
with the matter otherwise. I cannot deal with observations made upon an amendment until the order for resuming the debate on that particular subject is called by the clerk assistant. As to the fears expressed by the Leader of the Opposition that perhaps discussion might be curtailed on the first item of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the committee to supply, may I say that I do not think he should entertain those fears. As I recall it, on the first item of a department in supply the discussion is always allowed to cover all the administration of that department.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext: Under those terms, Mr. Speaker, the situation is entirely satisfactory in any event.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext:
There is another point that I should like to take care of and that has to do with the remarks that were made at the beginning of our sittings today with respect to the amendment to the motion to go into supply which is on the order paper for Monday next. Upon reflection, I see now why the matter was brought up by the Leader of the Opposition. We are to go into committee of supply without question put, and the first department to be called is trade and commerce, the first item being administration. Under that first item of course comes perhaps the matter of wheat. Yesterday we had a debate initiated with respect to wheat on the motion to go into supply, which was adjourned last night, and which appears on the order paper for Monday next, item No. 3.
I do not want the house to be misled by what I said earlier. It is true that on the first item of any department in supply a general discussion of the department's activities is allowed. However, it would seem to me that the amendment moved to the motion to go into supply yesterday is blocking a discussion with respect to wheat today in the committee of supply on the first item of trade and commerce. Citation 246 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms says:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 41, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(d) anticipate discussion on a motion set down for future consideration.

Business of the House
Anyone dealing with wheat would certainly be anticipating discussion of the motion which is set down on the order paper for Monday next.
Furthermore, hon. members are limited by the terms of standing order 40(2), which is to the effect that one must not repeat arguments of his own or arguments used by others. I just want to point out that there is this difficulty at this stage of the proceedings in connection with the subject of wheat.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext:
Before we pass from that, may I say that Your Honour has apprehended the very difficulty that I anticipated. I would point out that it is not the choice of the opposition that we broke from the motion that was before the house to discuss trade and commerce.
I would point out that by the device of halting a debate before it is concluded and then calling a department which embraces the subject matter of a motion of that kind we could find ourselves denied the opportunity to discuss it at all, that is further than the discussion which has already taken place, because, as I pointed out earlier, Your Honour did indicate some uncertainty as to what was in your mind. I am prepared to argue that point because I submit the point is in order. Nevertheless, Your Honour indicated quite clearly last night that you thought the motion might be out of order. In that event we might find ourselves foreclosed from the possibility of discussing an extremely important aspect of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and then find when we returned on Monday that Your Honour had come to the conclusion that he thought it was not in order and that the very motion which is now being discussed on this subject is in fact not a valid barrier at all.
I would repeat that the choice by which that debate was suspended and we now come into trade and commerce was not our choice. I am not suggesting for one moment that the course which has been followed is one that was designed for that purpose. I would point out, however, that the government, which has nothing to do with that, could by that very method interfere with the ordinary discussion of a subject before the house and I submit that while hon. members might well refrain from the detailed discussion of this subject which has already come forward, that if we talk on trade and commerce we can hardly take the time to deal with it in its all-embracing aspects without considering the impact of the present wheat situation upon trade and commerce in Canada.
I do submit, Mr. Speaker, that if your ruling were to be that the mere introduction

of the subject of the wheat surplus were to be suspended or could not be proceeded with because of the adjournment of that motion, then some course should be followed which would open the door to discussion because we would be having a discussion on the first item on the Department of Trade and Commerce under very unsatisfactory conditions. It must of necessity be with the consent of the house, but because of the importance of this matter I would be prepared to withdraw the motion we were debating yesterday for the purpose of overcoming any difficulties of this kind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say just a word or two on this? On Tuesday on the opposition side of the house there was a general feeling that this was a matter of urgency and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) both attempted to introduce a motion to that effect. We urged the government to vary the business but the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) could not see his way clear to do so. He said then, with respect to the urgency of discussing this matter, as reported at page 5624 of Hansard for that day:
The most I would be prepared to suggest is that either when we move to go into supply at a time when that motion is to be debated or when we get into supply, the first department called be the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext: Either.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext:
Quite so. But he indicated that the matter of urgency was to be met when the first department was the Department of Trade and Commerce. We are in a bit of a muddle this morning regarding procedure, Mr. Speaker, but under the first item as a rule the discussion is very wide and I myself can see no objection to the house debating the wheat problem under the Department of Trade and Commerce and even concluding that debate, so that when we get back to a supply motion all that would have to be done would be to receive Your Honour's ruling on the amendment and the subamendment and if you so allow a vote can be taken at that time.
It seems to me, in the situation in which we are, that that would be the sensible thing for the house to do, but it is a matter for the house and yourself, Mr. Speaker, rather than for any individual in this house to decide as regards what is to be done. But I am making that suggestion to the house and to you, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that is a way out of the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Leader of the C.C.F. party has explained the situation, as I understand it, quite clearly. In response to the desire of hon. members opposite that this matter might be debated at an early time the government did say it was going to call the Department of Trade and Commerce first on, I think, two successive days, giving them the opportunity when we got into supply. I presume hon. members are aware of the rule which provides that on Thursdays and Fridays we can discuss these matters without question put, and the opposition members have an option of taking whatever action they desire with that in mind. However, since all the hon. members who have spoken so far seem to be desirous of disposing of the matter the alternative presented by that hon. member would be acceptable to the government, that is if it is the desire of the house the amendment be now dropped so that it would not be called on Monday and we would agree to debate wheat or any other subject on this item. On the other hand, if the suggestion made by the leader of the C.C.F. party is adopted, that is that we debate the subject now by consent, and that there is to be no further debate on the amendments on Monday, then we are content.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY-SUGGESTED PROCEDURE FOR DISPOSAL

May I suggest to the acting leader of the government that although we can go into supply on Thursdays and Fridays without question put, what he could do is to suspend the standing order so that we can then go into supply with question put today and move that item 3 be taken and then I will by my ruling dispose of the two amendments, the main motion will carry, and we will go into supply.

We go into supply Thursdays and Fridays without question put although, if it was the wish of hon. members to have a debate on the motion to go into supply by suspending the provisions of the standing order, a motion could be made and we could have a debate on the motion to go into supply. If it is unanimously agreed that this be done then immediately I make my ruling and the two amendments are disposed of-and I take it that is the wish of hon. members-the motion could then be carried and I would leave the chair and the house could go into committee of supply on the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subsubtopic: ITALY-ARRANGEMENT REGARDING CODFISH, CANNED SALMON AND SYNTHETIC RUBBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to
make an important announcement to the house. Wednesday evening a joint statement was issued in Rome by the Hon. Mario Mar-tinelli, minister of foreign trade of Italy, and the Hon. Robert Winters, Minister of Public Works of Canada. This statement announced an arrangement between Canada and Italy whereby Italy has agreed to make dollars available for the importation of codfish, canned salmon and synthetic rubber. This arrangement was negotiated by Hon. Robert

Winters, following preliminary discussions carried on in Rome with Italian officials by Shirley G. MacDonald, commercial counsellor of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Under this arrangement the government of Italy has agreed to make dollars available for the purchase during the period July 1, 1954, to June 30, 1955, of Newfoundland and Labrador type codfish valued at $2,500,000, Gaspe type codfish valued at $600,000 and canned salmon valued at $2,000,000. Provision for the sale of canned salmon was made possible by the lower prices for this product now being quoted in markets abroad. In addition, an initial quota for the importation of $500,000 worth of synthetic rubber has been established. This quota is over and above the considerable quantity of synthetic rubber for which quotas have already been established.
Codfish, canned salmon and synthetic rubber are among the most important Canadian exports to Italy. This new arrangement will place sales of these products on a firm and stable basis in the Italian market.

minor additional section in the new regulations providing for the continuation of the seamen's cards and of the forms prescribed by the Minister of Labour issued and used under the old regulations. Provision also is to be made for the revocation of the old regulations. It is proposed that this additional section shall read as follows:
24 (1) A provisional or regular seaman's card issued under the great lakes seamen's security regulations, established by order in council P.C. 2306 of May 2, 1952 (hereinafter called the old regulations) shall be deemed to have been issued under these regulations, and a form prescribed by the minister under the old regulations shall be deemed to have been prescribed by the minister under these regulations.
(2) The old regulations shall be deemed to have been revoked and these regulations shall be deemed to have been substituted therefor, and the Interpretation Act applies accordingly.
The house will note that this does not in any way change the substance of the old i egulations in any detail. My only reason for rising is that we made a firm declaration yesterday that there would be no immediate change in the old regulations.

It introduces a loose, improper, and in our opinon, a method of control inconsistent with our traditions. The fact that there was an order in council to this effect under the Emergency Powers Act, which came into being during the war emergency, does not in our opinion support the suggestion that the house should now give to the government in statutory form the power to make regulations, to decide what the penalty will be and to decide how the freedom of the individual will be dealt with.
We have made it clear that we are strongly of the opinion that proper laws, clearly defined, should be available to deal with this situation where people are seeking to undermine our free system in Canada. We believe, however, the freedom of any individual should at no time be threatened by star chamber proceedings or by proceedings which are of an undefined and undisclosed nature. We have placed that on the record. We believe the principle inherent in this piece of legislation is vicious. What justification there may have been for the order in council under the Emergency Powers Act, and which was apparent during the war emergency, I submit that there can be no support for the 83276-365i
Navigable Waters Protection Act enactment in clear statutory form of these loose powers so long described as the King Henry VIII clause. This is a reversion to a practice that disappeared 400 years ago. We should not revive it today in specific form.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that the same be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they delete clause 2 thereof.

Righl Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Chairman, as in past years, I shall introduce the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce with a short review of recent trade developments as they affect Canada.
Last year I said that 1953 might well bring forth a number of far-reaching decisions and
[Mr. Maclnnls.l

important developments in the field of international trade relations. I think that I can now safely say that this has indeed been the case. Because of the decisions taken and the policies adopted in a number of important trading countries we have good reason to believe that we are, in many instances, rapidly moving towards the kind of trading relations we have been striving for since the end of the war. There are still many substantial obstacles to be overcome. However, the unprecedented progress of the past year has brought the ultimate objective of relatively unhampered multilateral trade much closer.
For the first time in many years we have concrete evidence that many of the world's trading nations are increasingly prepared to remove their restrictions against imports from the dollar area. The countries of the commonwealth, which account for a substantial proportion of world trade, reaffirmed at the Sydney finance ministers conference their support for the objectives of a freer system of multilateral trade. Closely following this conference a number of significant relaxations were made in the import controls of important sterling countries. In addition, the signatories to the general agreement on tariffs and trade decided in October, 1953, to maintain intact the tariff concessions bound under the general agreement.
In the United States the Randall commission submitted its report to the President on United States foreign economic and trade policy. The commission's recommendations, while perhaps not going as far as we would wish, nevertheless are largely constructive and progressive. Although it now appears that congress may not take immediate action to implement these recommendations, no doubt responsible leaders in congress and elsewhere in the United States will wish to see the commission's findings brought into force as quickly as possible.
There is, of course, a great deal of interest in and concern about the increasing protectionist pressures in the United States. There is no need to dramatize these developments by assuming that a trade war is about to break out between Canada and the United States. We are the largest customer of the United States as they are ours. I do not expect a trade war, either cold or hot, as long as we continue on both sides of the border to remember the strong interest of both countries in trading on a neighbourly basis. Our trade agreements with the United States have been negotiated as business deals. Concessions have been received and concessions have been granted and the resulting balance has been of mutual benefit to both countries.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
It would, of course, be a matter of regret if the United States government were to take the initiative in adopting measures which would have the result of impairing U.S. trade with Canada and other friendly countries. But I give the overwhelming majority of the people of the United States credit for not wanting this to happen any more than we do. It should therefore be our policy to conduct ourselves in such a way as to give help to those who share our views and to show those who would withdraw concessions negotiated in good faith that such action is not in the interests of the United States.
It is noteworthy that progress in trade matters in the non-dollar world coincided with a decline in business activity in the United States. Despite this fact, sales to the United States from soft currency countries have not shown any appreciable decline. In fact, the sterling area has not only maintained its level of business with the United States but the pound is now stronger than it has been for many years and dollar and gold reserves held in London have reached record post-war levels. This development is in sharp contrast to the past unfavourable influences of United States business fluctuations on trade. It reflects, I believe, the underlying strength of the movement towards the recovery of world trade on a multilateral basis.
As the committee is well aware, Canada has consistently expressed its view that the creation of exclusive regional arrangements, trading behind protective barriers, distorts the economies of the countries following such practices and leads to inefficiency and high costs. The economic security which seems to result from such arrangements is of short duration and illusory in a competitive world. These facts have brought an increasing number of non-dollar countries to recognize that these arrangements and restrictive trade policies create more problems than they solve. In their own interest many non-dollar countries are increasingly prepared to relax their trade and exchange restrictions, and to move forward with plans for the eventual convertibility of their currency.
The United Kingdom, Canada's second best customer, has made extensive progress in removing import restrictions from agricultural, mineral and wood products. As a result of these important steps, about 70 per cent of Canada's exports to the United Kingdom, based on 1953 trade statistics, enter that country freely and are not subject to governmental restriction. Although most of the products thus freed from control are of a primary nature, we hope that the United Kingdom will soon relax its restrictions on goods in semi-processed and other categories.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Other countries of the sterling area have also taken significant steps to remove import controls which have discriminated against dollar goods. At Geneva last fall South Africa announced the removal of all discriminatory import restrictions. Since January 1 of this year Canadians have therefore had an opportunity to sell in the South African market on an equal footing with exporters of other countries.
New Zealand, Australia and the British West Indies have also recently announced important measures relaxing their restrictions against dollar goods. In the case of New Zealand in particular, these relaxations have affected an extensive variety of Canadian products.
The trend to freer trade has not been limited to commonwealth countries. In Europe, The Netherlands and Germany have freed many dollar imports from restrictions. Other European countries are actively studying the possibility of reducing their discriminatory controls on trade. In Latin America a number of Canada's important customers have also relaxed their trade restrictions against dollar imports. Among these countries are Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Colombia.
These developments are indeed encouraging, particularly when it is considered that they have been accompanied by a striking improvement in the internal and external financial position of these countries. In their external relations, most countries enjoyed increased exports and a more favourable balance of payments with the dollar area. The sterling area alone has increased its reserves by $672 million during 1953.
I believe that there is a close relationship between these remarkable results and the adoption of sound trading and internal policies. The gradual reduction of import controls, imposed for protective reasons, and the widespread trend to eliminate restrictions which have discriminated against dollar goods has undoubtedly improved the competitive position of the countries which have adopted such policies. It is significant to note that in 1953 the United Kingdom was able to increase its sales to Canada by $94 million over the previous year. This is an increase of 21 per cent; it also increased the United Kingdom's share of Canada's purchases from external sources from 9 per cent in 1952 to 10 per cent in 1953.
The remarkable strengthening of the United Kingdom's trading and financial position during the past year has undoubtedly placed that country in a much better position to place its currency on a convertible basis. It is, of course, impossible to say when this may happen since this decision can be made only
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).!
by the government of the United Kingdom when it feels that its position is sufficiently strong to take this major step.
The recently concluded agreement on commerce with Japan represents a further advance in our efforts to create abroad better conditions for our exporters. We have established a mutually satisfactory basis for our trade with that country on terms which will ensure favourable treatment for Canadian exporters while safeguarding the interests of our manufacturers. In 1953 Japan was our third largest customer, buying nearly $119 million of Canadian products. This agreement will no doubt provide a permanent basis for the maintenance of high levels of Canadian trade with Japan.
As I mentioned a few moments ago, Canada has been a consistent advocate of multilateral trade. One of the major means by which we have actively implemented this policy has been through our participation in the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Last fall I had the pleasure of leading the Canadian delegation to the eighth session of the contracting parties to GATT. I welcomed the decisions reached there to maintain intact the whole structure of tariff concessions that had been negotiated by more than thirty countries over the last several years.
At the eighth session tentative arrangements were made for a review of the provisions of GATT at some appropriate time in the future. The general provisions of the agreement were originally intended to be of a temporary nature. Many countries, including Canada, now feel that they should be reconsidered and revised in a manner more consistent and more appropriate to present-day circumstances.

The review of GATT, whenever it takes place, will be greatly influenced not only

by the experience gained in recent years but also by the policy matters now being formulated by the major trading countries. In this regard the role of the United States is of primary importance. The success or failure of any new steps is almost certain to depend on whether that country is in a position to give constructive leadership. If a review session is successfully held it may be found possible and desirable to subsequently conduct further tariff negotiations on a mutually beneficial basis.
During the forthcoming year major decisions hang in the balance. To a large extent these will decide whether or not the gains of the past year will be maintained and expanded still further. One of the most important factors in this balance is the future of United States commercial policy. If the United States is in a position to actively sponsor the expansion of trade and to implement this policy with appropriate legislation, there can be little doubt that the way will be open to the further expansion of trade. On the other hand, if the measures currently before congress are not implemented, and if steps to restrict imports are adopted, it will be indeed difficult to look to the future with optimism.
Let me turn now to the facts of our trading position. First, however, let me say a word about the general business situation. It has been evident for some time that the Canadian economy has been affected by the downturn in the United States which has been under way since mid-1953. Production and employment in Canada have declined moderately from the peak levels reached last year, although the reduction has been less pronounced than in the United States. In Canada, as in the United States, the slowdown in business purchasing, resulting in inventory liquidation in some lines, has been an important factor. This type of adjustment is usually self-correcting in character unless it is accompanied by a more general weakening in consumer demand or in investment or export demand. Fortunately consumer spending and private capital outlays in Canada have remained reasonably firm. In fact, of the major demands on the Canadian economy only exports have shown signs of falling off. Accordingly, I intend to limit my remarks at this time to a brief review of matters affecting our foreign trade.
For more than a year Canada's exports have shown a slight downward trend. In 1953 the value of Canadian exports amounted to $4,117 million compared with $4,301 million in 1952, a decline of 4 per cent. In the first quarter of the present year exports
Supply-Trade and Commerce have undergone a further moderate reduction of about 5 per cent. Since prices are a little lower, the decline in terms of physical volume is somewhat smaller.
Any decline is of course unwelcome, but it should be borne in mind that this slight falling off in exports followed several years of substantial increases. Total sales abroad in the past year are still 15 per cent above the 1949 level in volume terms. This is about the same as the percentage rise in the national output during the same period. It considerably exceeds the increase in the volume of world trade. In other words, since 1949 Canada has continued to increase her share of sales in the international markets.
The fact that other nations are relying to an increasing extent upon Canada as a source of supply, especially for basic materials, is an important factor in our present expansion. But there are other reasons for Canada's growth. While much of the new burst of expansion, which occurred after Korea, was for the production of goods to be sold abroad, a major portion of the new capacity created in recent years has had the effect of replacing imports. The spectacular expansion in oil, natural gas and steel will, in the course of a few years, involve hundreds of millions of dollars less expenditures for imported materials. This type of development could, over the course of time, permit a relative shift of resources toward production for the domestic market.
This development does not, of course significantly lessen the importance of foreign trade to Canada. The nature of our resources is such that we shall always find it profitable to specialize heavily in the production of certain products and sell abroad the excess over and above our own needs.
Nevertheless as the size and industrial structure of the economy changes, the role of foreign trade will also change to some extent. In some periods a stable or even slightly declining level of exports is not necessarily indicative of a basic weakening in the economy. The tendency to gauge our economic strength solely on the basis of the movement of exports is, I think, a dangerous oversimplification of the forces which shape our development. 1 cannot see that our basic economic strength is substantially different now from what it was two or three years ago when export levels were rising at a rapid rate. There are of course other more temporary influences which have had an important bearing on current trends in our export trade.
One such influence has been the extraordinary conditions which have affected wheat

Supply-Trade and Commerce sales in recent years. In the two crop year periods ending July 31, 1953, the unusual combination of record crops in Canada and a strong world market boosted Canadian sales of wheat and flour to an annual average of 371 million bushels. This was 142 million bushels above average exports for the precedi g 20-year period. The wheat situation was reviewed in detail by the agricultural committee, but I state these figures here simply to indicate the extent to which higher sales of wheat contributed to the sharp rise in exports during this period.

speechtext:
I think I can leave it at what has been said. Another factor which has had a depressing effect on exports during the last six to nine months has been the declining level of activity in the United States economy. The importance of this influence will be apparent when we realize that in 1953 sales to the United States accounted for 59 per cent of our total exports. Nevertheless, the prevalent view among those who follow the United States economic situation is that the current recession has about run its course after a decline of 10 per cent in industrial output and 3 per cent in gross national product from the peak levels reached in 1953. If this is to be the full extent of the present decline, the recession has, by historic standards, been a relatively mild one.
Moreover, the effect on Canadian exports has been less by reason of the fact that the pulp and paper market and activity in the United States construction industry have remained comparatively firm throughout the adjustment. Wood products as a group account for 45 per cent of total Canadian sales in the United States market. Some other export items have not fared so well. Durable goods industries in the United States have been hardest hit by the downturn and this tended to accentuate the softening already under way in the international base metal market. Consequently, exports of copper, lead and zinc have shown an appreciable decline. More recently, however, some firming in demand for these items has occurred.
Business conditions have, in general, remained prosperous in most of the overseas areas which provide markets for Canadian goods. In the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan, which outside the United States are Canada's most important customers, industrial activity has been increasing and this, in turn, has helped to support purchasing of raw materials and foodstuffs from Canada. While exports to the United Kingdom declined last year the latest trade figures available show a major improvement in sales to this market compared with a year ago.
Conditions have not been universally favourable in all non-dollar markets. Exchange difficulties have been acute in seme Latin American countries. In addition, increasingly competitive conditions have been encountered in this market, especially
Supply-Trade and Commerce in the manufactured goods field. As a result Canadian exports to Latin America have declined considerably from the peak level reached in 1952 but are still running above sales of any previous year.
Looking at exports by commodity groups, markets for the principal forest products are generally firm. Consumption of newsprint in the United States has continued to increase slightly, inventories are not excessive and it is expected that this market will absorb at least the same amount of Canadian newsprint this year as last. The United States market for wood pulp has strengthened appreciably and sales are now running well ahead of a year ago. In overseas countries purchases from Canada are increasing. Canadian lumber is meeting sharp competition in the United States and so far this year sales to that country have been down moderately. Nevertheless, building activity in the United States has continued to increase, and this will be an important influence supporting the demand for Canadian lumber. In addition, there are firm prospects for substantially increased sales of lumber this year to the United Kingdom and other overseas countries. While certain other wood products, particularly plywood, are in easy supply position, it seems likely that exports of forest products as a whole will show a moderate increase in 1954. Since sales have held about even in the first quarter this would involve some improvement during the remainder of the year.
In the metals field, firm markets exist for Canada's output of nickel and aluminum. World supplies of other base metals have for some time been more than adequate to meet current needs and production cutbacks have occurred in several major producing areas. It is possible that in the months ahead sales will show some improvement. Before the end of the year it is expected that iron ore from Quebec-Labrador will be moving into the great lakes market adding to the already increasing volume of shipments from Steep Rock and Algoma ore properties. With the construction of new pipe line outlets the volume of Canadian crude oil moving into the United States will be considerably increased by the end of the year.
There has been some broadening out of our foreign markets for fish products during the past year. For the first time in several years Brazil now permits imports of salt cod from Canada. We have negotiated new trade agreements with Spain and Portugal which enlarge our opportunities to sell salt cod in those markets. The United Kingdom again

Supply-Trade and Commerce this year is making a large purchase of B.C. salmon while both Australia and New Zealand have made a dollar allocation for the purchase of this product from Canada.
The one commodity group, apart from grains, likely to encounter a significant decline in export values this year is highly manufactured commodities such as automobiles, farm machinery, textile and leather goods and industrial, commercial and electrical equipment. As for farm machinery, demand in the United States market, which accounts for most of Canada's exports, has declined in line with the downward trend of farm income and also as a result of the unusually large purchases in recent years which have left farmers well stocked with equipment. The decline in exports of highly manufactured products taken as a group should, I think, be considered in the light of certain changes in the pattern of world trade generally. For one thing, in commonwealth countries and in other such traditional markets for Canadian manufactured goods, further industrialization has meant that these products are now in many cases produced domestically. Another important point is that in the years since world war II and even during the Korean episode the shortage of manufactured goods available from traditional sources such as the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan meant that Canada was able temporarily to participate in markets in which we would not have been able to compete in more normal circumstances.
It is, I think, important to remember that countries which are highly industrialized but scarce in natural resources depend largely on foreign sales of manufactured products to enable them to buy the large quantities of raw materials and food which they must obtain from outside their borders. We must remember also that their costs are geared to this necessity. With more capacity becoming available in these highly industrialized countries, and with demand for manufactured products tending to level off, Canadian manufacturers have found it increasingly difficult to compete in world markets. Such a situation should provide no particular cause for alarm. Canada does not lack for export opportunities and it is not necessary or even desirable for Canadian producers to be able to compete in world markets in all lines of merchandise. In our principal staple export items, Canadian producers are highly competitive the world over. So long as this is the case there is little basically wrong with our foreign trade position.
Increasing world supplies of manufactured goods have brought more competitive conditions in the domestic market as well as

abroad. While imports increased substantially last year, especially in the early months, so far this year purchases from abroad have declined more than exports. The 7 per cent drop in imports in the first quarter considerably exceeds the reduction in total production and employment for the same period. This means that, for the time being at least, there has been an increase of the share of the home market going to the domestic producer, which is in sharp contrast to the trend one year ago. However, even with this smaller volume of imports, there is little evidence of any significant easing in the pressure of competition from foreign producers.
Mr. Chairman, I have attempted to explain some of the principal influences underlying recent trade trends. In spite of some adverse influences I think one can conclude that Canada's present export position is, on the whole, firmly based. I continue to be optimistic about the future of the Canadian economy.

In approaching this present debate it is not perhaps amiss to remind ourselves that we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and that those estimates propose the expenditure on account of this department, along with the supplementary estimates, of the sum of $18,789,654 for the year 1953-54 as compared with a total of $17,316,971 last year. In other words, the estimates of this year on behalf of this department call for an increase in expenditure of approximately $1,470,000.
This department, from the point of view of expenditure, is a relatively stable one. Its expenditures do not vary greatly from year to year. While its expenditures are substantial, this department is not one of the big spending departments of government.

The stability o f which I have made mention is also reflected in the size of the staff of the department. The report of the department for the calendar year 1953 indicates that the staff within the department, excluding the board of grain commissioners, the Canadian government elevators and the dominion bureau of statistics, is 1,197, which is one more that in the year 1952, and precisely the same figure as in the year 1951. The figures also on staff of the three organizations to which I have referred, the board of grain commissioners, the Canadian government elevators and the dominion bureau of statistics, are also relatively stable, bringing the total to 3,669 for the year 1953.
This present debate on trade will, I take it, not range over the entire field of our trading relations with the world. In the first place, we had an extensive debate on trade with Japan when the house debated the motion for ratification of the trade treaty with Japan on May 12, and there has been some discussion already in the house yesterday on the matter of wheat, which of course occupies a position of leading importance in all of Canada's export trade plans.
The subject of Canada's trade and commerce is one of first importance to every Canadian. Twenty-five per cent of Canada's national production goes to the export market. Our per capita share of the trade of the world is exceeded by only two countries, namely, New Zealand and Hong Kong. Last year Canada's total trade, both export and import, at $8,500 million means that with a population of 15 million, each Canadian had a share of approximately $560 in the total Canadian external trade. While I have not seen the final world trade figures for 1953 in relation to the position occupied by the various countries, I believe it is a fact that Canada did continue to occupy third place among the trading nations of the world, as she did in 1952, exceeded only by the United States and the United Kingdom.
Now, sir, we have had the minister's statement on this subject. The minister's statements are always interesting, but they do follow a very pronounced and typical pattern. Without being unfairly critical one might say that the minister's statement this morning was typical. It was a selective statement. No room was found in it for reference to the extensive unemployment that exists in Canada today. No mention was made in it, for instance, of the fact that last week several of the auto manufactories of this country
Supply-Trade and Commerce were obliged to suspend their present operations. Indeed, the minister did succeed in glossing over, without spending too much time on them, those factors in the external trade situation that do give every thoughtful Canadian very serious concern at the present time. To the extent to which the minister permitted himself even to concede the existence of such factors, his remarks were intended to discount the extent and importance of them. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it is not unfair to say that the minister's statement, as on so many occasions, finishing as it did, with the note of optimism, was characterized by the Nelson touch. The minister did succeed in putting his glass to the blind eye that the minister has been found to possess in matters relating to Canada's external trade that ought to be giving us concern. The minister simply does not see those.
Canada's external trade has not changed in relation to the problems it presents, has not changed since we debated the subject on the first item of the minister's estimates in this house a little over a year ago. Certainly, as I see the problem, rightly or wrongly, the problem is essentially the same as I attempted to describe it in speaking in that debate on April 22, 1953. The problem, however, has developed in the intervening 14 months, and the developments have followed lines that were visible at that time. It has followed the course of which I think those of us in this part of the house sought to warn the house and the government at that time.
I know that figures are not the most interesting subject to follow; nevertheless we cannot validly estimate the trends or the problems that face Canada in relation to her external trade without due reflection upon the figures of exports and imports. I have here a table which I prepared from government sources concerning Canada's exports and imports for the years 1952 and 1953, arranged in terms of the total figures and also in terms of percentage. I am not asking any consideration of the committee in this regard. If it would be more convenient to have this table on the records of the house instead of my reading it I would be quite pleased to deal with it on that basis. Perhaps it might save a little time.

What is evident from these figures as to Canada's export and import trade in 1952 and in 1953 can be summed up in the terms of these important trends. The minister referred to one or two in his remarks on the import side. I think we are principally concerned with our trade with the United Kingdom and with the United States, and the position they hold as a percentage of world trade. In 1952, Canada imported from the United Kingdom [The Deputy Chairman.]
$360 million worth of goods, and that represented 9 per cent of our total imports. In 1953, as the minister mentioned, the figure increased to $453 million and the percentage to 10-3. That was an increase which I think we all welcomed. I go further, Mr. Chairman, and say that I think we would all welcome a much greater increase. From the commonwealth there was no very material change in either value or percentage of our imports as between 1952 and 1953.
However, from the United States in 1952 we imported goods to the value of $2,977 million, and in 1953 $3,221 million, and our percentage in the two cases remained uniform at 74 per cent of the total. In the grand total our imports for 1952 were $4,030 million and they increased to $4,383 million in 1953.
On the export side, we see that our exports to the United Kingdom showed a drop in 1953 as compared with 1952, from $746 million in 1952 to $665 million in 1953, and they also show that the percentage dropped from 17-3 per cent to 16-1 per cent. Our exports to the commonwealth remained stable in the two years both as to amount and percentage.
But to the United States our exports in 1952 were $2,307 million and in 1953 rose to $2,419 million. Similarly, because the total of Canadian exports last year was reduced from $4,301 million in 1952 to $4,117 million in 1953 the percentage of exports to the United States showed a substantial increase, rising from 53 [DOT] 5 per cent in 1952 to 59 per cent in 1953.
Before I leave this comparison in trade figures for these two years, Mr. Chairman, I think it is interesting to look at them in relation to two other subjects. The first is where we stand in regard to the over-all surplus. In 1952 Canada had an export surplus, or what used to be called a favourable balance of trade, of $271 million, but in 1953 that had changed and we no longer had an export surplus. We had what is now called an import surplus, or what we used to call an unfavourable balance of trade, of $266 million.
I leave this subject with this one further observation, Mr. Chairman, that in looking at the percentage of our total trade, whether export or import, occupied by the United Kingdom on the one hand, and the United States on the other, it will be seen that in 1952 we did 63-4 per cent of our total external trade with the United States. In 1953 that percentage had risen to 67 per cent. In other words, in 1953 we were doing slightly

more than two-thirds of our total external trade with one country, namely, the United States.
The figures for the United Kingdom on the other hand show that the percentage of our total trade that we did with the United Kingdom in 1952 was 13-3 per cent, and that that has fallen slightly in 1953 to 13-1 per cent of the total.
As to the first four months of 1954, for which the figures are available, our export trade has undergone a further decrease, and our import trade has likewise shown a decrease. The export figures for the first four months of the year have dropped from $1,219 million in 1953 to $1,164 million in 1954. Our imports are down from $1,390 million in 1953 to $1,282 million in the first four months of 1954. Our exports to the United States in this four-month period show a slight decrease of $48 million. Our exports to the United Kingdom show a slight increase of $5 million. Our imports from the United Kingdom show a decrease of $9 million, and our imports from the United States show a decrease of $104 million.
Now I hope I have not wearied the house with that review of what seem to me to be very important figures. They show unmistakably the existence of certain trends.
First, there is a continuing drop in Canada's over-all external trade. That drop has now been continuing for some 16 months up to the end of the period to which I referred, namely, April 30, 1954.
Second, the drop in exports began sooner and is still continuing, and in that over-all period of some 16 months the drop in exports has considerably exceeded the proportionate drop in imports.
Third, Canada has incurred in the period in question an adverse balance of trade, in other words, what is now called an import balance. That import balance continued throughout the whole period of 1953 and has continued in the first four months of 1954, because in this first four months of 1954 our imports exceeded our exports by $118 million.
Fourth, our trade with the United States simply dwarfs our trade with all other countries, whether taken individually or combined, to an extent which is daily becoming more serious and more perilous for Canada. Our trade eggs are being placed in one basket and that basket is by no means the most certain or satisfactory trade basket in the light of history.
Fifth, with that one country, namely the United States, we have today an adverse
Supply-Trade and Commerce balance of trade which, in the period I have been discussing, has almost set records. An adverse balance of commodity trade on the part of Canada in relation to the United States is not new. It is an historic fact. But now the extent of it is so great as to call for the most serious examination on the part of all Canadians.
Sixth, on an examination of the nature of our trade, it will be seen, I think, that it is in relation to our agricultural products, that so vulnerable feature of Canada's economy, that the problems to which I have referred appear for Canada in their most serious aspect.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

Mr. Chairman, following my review of the figures of external trade of the past two years and four months, I should like to turn now to examine more closely our trading relationships with certain countries. I pass over our trading relationships with Japan because of the extensive discussion we had on that subject on May 12.
Lately there have been tabled in the house copies of new trade agreements with Portugal and with Spain; and the minister this morning announced the signing yesterday in Rome of a trade agreement with Italy. May I say at once that so far as these trade treaties offer hope of increasing the shipments principally of Canadian dried salt codfish to these countries, these agreements will, of course, be welcomed. We shall be glad indeed to see any opportunities provided for extending Canadian exports, particularly in the commodities principally affected by these treaties.
I now turn to our trade with the United Kingdom. In the last year before the war we sent to the United Kingdom 35-5 per cent of our total exports. In 1953 we sent to the United Kingdom just 16-1 per cent of our total exports. I am aware of the fact that percentages do not always tell the whole story but nevertheless it seems to me that there is here reason for concern. Great Britain has been our best market; it has been our traditional market, particularly for our agricultural surplus. It is because of that fact that it is so important that we retain the British market. The fact of the matter is, however, that over a period of years we have been losing the British market for many of our principal food products. That market is virtually closed to our shipments of bacon,
5772	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce pork, beef and apples. Our shipments of fish to that market are much smaller than they used to be. Our shipments of cheese are only a fraction of what they used to be. Our shipments of wheat to that country are down substantially in volume and value.
But, Mr. Chairman, this loss of the British market does not seem yet to give the government any worry. In the face of this alarming loss of the British market for our agricultural surplus, if one could see on the part of the government some evidence of concern, some evidence that the situation worries them, and that they might for that reason want to exert heroic efforts to recover that market, then one would not be disposed to view the situation with the same alarm as one must when one sees on the part of the government, in the face of this loss of our best traditional market, what appears to be complete indifference and resignation. We in this part of the chamber do not view the loss of the British market, particularly for our agricultural surplus, with any degree of resignation. We conceive it to be the duty of the government to exert every effort within its power to seek to recover that lost market.
There are various ways in which that desirable end can be furthered. Mr. James S. Duncan, the chairman of the dollar-sterling trade council, in a statement which he issued on April 14, drew attention to the desirability of increasing our purchases from the United Kingdom. In that statement he said:
"Based on last year's trade pattern, if we could transfer only 7 per cent of our imports from the United States to the United Kingdom, it would eliminate Britain's trade deficit with us and put her in a much better position to buy our products," said Mr. Duncan. The council's purpose is to assist in this 7 per cent transfer of imports.
Mr. Chairman, 7 per cent does not look like a large percentage; yet the striking fact is that if we brought about a transfer of 7 per cent of our purchases from the United States to the United Kingdom we would in that way close up Britain's trade deficit with us and put her in possession of dollars with which to buy here goods that she needs.
In his recent visit to this country Mr. Peter Thorneycroft, president of the British board of trade, drew attention to the fact that Britain desires to increase her purchases from Canada and also to increase her investments in Canada. But, as he strikingly put it, you cannot invest a deficit; you cannot invest a deficit either in terms of capital investment or in terms of consumer or capital goods. We should therefore like to see some evidence on the part of the government of a realistic appreciation of this fact and a realistic approach to it. We do not, however, find either.


Mention was made this morning by the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the fact that the internal position of Britain within the sterling bloc has strengthened greatly, particularly during the past year. Britain's trading and financial position within the sterling area has certainly strengthened materially. In the face of that fact, we may hope that the day of the restoration of the convertibility of currency may be eventually coming within sight. Indeed, the recent agreement entered into by Mr. Butler with the government of the West German republic seems to indicate that Britain is now moving by steady stages in the direction of the removal of trade restrictions and also of some of the currency restrictions which hitherto have been applied. Be that as it may, Mr. Chairman, the fact is that unless we become more seriously alive to the dangers to our economy resulting from the loss of the British market we are courting a danger particularly for the basic industry of agriculture in this country.
Other nations are not standing idly by and ignoring the importance of the British market. In recent months we have seen evidence of the desire of Russia to expand her trade with Great Britain. Indeed some rather striking statements have been emanating from Russia about the desire to extend trade with Great Britain, and there have been placed in Britain by the Russian government important orders for machinery and other British industrial products. But, Mr. Chairman, what of the other side of this possible trade between Britain and Russia? This is something which is of direct concern to Canada. I call the attention of hon. members to a statement made on March 23 of this year in the House of Commons at Westminster by Mr. Derick Heathcoat-Amory, the British minister of overseas trade, when he said this:
The British market is "wide open to Russian grain, timber, metals and manganese ore".
Speaking in debate on east-west trade, he said it would be "very helpful if larger quantities of grain could be made available".
Canada has almost unlimited quantities of grain that she would very much like to sell. Why is the government not making spirited efforts to see to it that it is to Canadian grain that the British purchaser turns rather than to Russian grain? There are, of course, questions of policy involved on the part of Britain in extending trade with Russia. It is thought that it may help to contribute toward peace if east-west trade is restored somewhat. But, Mr. Chairman, knowing that the Russians are prepared to sell Britain grain, and particularly wheat, what is Canada doing with this huge accumulation of wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are selling grain to Russia.
Oh, jolly little Canadian grain is going to Russia! You could almost put it in a hat.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, no. Two or
three ships are required.

Our trade with Russia has never been a serious factor in our external trade, but our trade with Great Britain has been a vital factor in our external trade. What we would like to see on the part of the government is a realistic appreciation of the necessity of claiming that British market, particularly for our grain products.
Now, sir, I turn to the subject of our trading relations with the United States. I drew attention this morning to the alarming extent to which our trading eggs have been placed in the American basket, to the fact that in 1953 a trifle over two-thirds of Canada's total external trade, both export and import, was done with this one country. We have some very serious problems facing us in reference to our trade with the United States. The mere size of that trade, the extent to which we seem to be putting our eggs in that one basket, is of itself cause for alarm, particularly when we have regard for the history of American trade in the past.
Last year we had an adverse balance of trade with the United States of around $800 million. That of itself, it seems to me, is also an alarming factor.
The next factor that should give us cause for deep concern is the fact that the United States, through government policies, has accumulated vast stores of agricultural products which are directly competitive with those of Canada. On March 17 of this year a statement emanated from Washington to the effect that before the United States embarked upon any policy of disposing of these surpluses in the external markets of the world there would be consultation with Canada. Well, sir, the fruits of the consultation are not very impressive indeed.
When we see what has happened within the past four or five days to the price of wheat 1 do not think anyone in the house can be impressed with the benefits of consultation. Consultation has not done very much in arriving at any policies that will be of benefit to the agricultural producers of Canada. The minister this morning in his review made reference to the Randall report. That report, which was submitted to the President of the United States on January 22 of this year, is a document which, so far as the majority on that commission was concerned, contained two principal recommendations to the president. The first was that there should be a
Supply-Trade and Commerce cut in American tariff rates of 5 per cent per annum for the next three years and, second, that there should be a three-year extension of the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act. That was the majority report.
The reaction within congress to that report so far has not been very encouraging. Indeed the problems faced by the president in relation to that report and in the way of implementation of its recommendations seem to be best demonstrated by the fact that there is no indication whatever at Washington that there is going to be any measure to cut tariff rates in the manner indicated, and also by the president's compromise with regard to the extension of the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act. The president has indicated to congress that he is prepared to accept a one-year extension of this act. Some papers have referred to this as a surrender on the part of the president. I do not know that that is an altogether fair judgment to pass, but in any event it is a compromise on the part of the president and it does serve to indicate the strength of the forces within the American congress who are going to seek to pursue policies that will create difficulties for the Canadian producer, particularly the producer of raw materials.
The next factor of serious concern for us in our trade relationship with the United States relates to the American attitude respecting the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Our experience in the past two and a half years as a signatory nation to GATT has been, so far as the United States is concerned, disquieting. We all regard the United States as a good neighbour, a sincere ally. We think that the cause to which the United States, Canada and the other nations of the free world are dedicating their efforts is a cause of good faith, good faith in dealings between men and good faith in dealings between nations. When the President of the United States, in pursuance of authority conferred upon him by the congress of the United States, enters into engagements with Canada and other nations signatories to GATT on behalf of the United States, it seems to Canadians that congress should be prepared to keep faith.
But, Mr. Chairman, the fact is that there have been on the part of the United States congress not one but several breaches of the provisions of GATT, breaches not simply of the spirit of GATT but breaches of the letter of GATT. We recall that in 1952, in breach of the provisions of GATT, the United States congress, through what is called the Andre-sen amendment, applied certain restrictions against the importation of Canadian dairy products. In 1953 those restrictions were

Supply-Trade and Commerce extended. Not long ago the Canadian government, at the request of the United States government, applied restrictions upon exports of Canadian oats to the United States.
I am not going to repeat what I have said on previous occasions with regard to this step taken by the Canadian government. I think it will suffice to say that in my view the Canadian government had no business, not only to acquiesce in the breach of GATT but to make itself a willing accomplice. The minister may say we might have had a difficult situation to face with the United States in view of the pressure that was being exerted upon the executive government down there to apply some form of tariff restriction on the importation of Canadian oats, but, Mr. Chairman, I affirm that it was no part of the duty of the Canadian government to come to the rescue of the American government under those conditions and itself apply restrictions upon the export of Canadian oats to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend will let me clear up a misconception in his mind. It is perfectly legitimate, under the provisions of GATT, to restrict the import of any commodity where the price is under price support, and oats are under price support. I agree that dairy products are not under price support and that was a violation of GATT, but when my hon. friend takes it into the field of oats, wheat, barley, flax and rye he is getting into a field where action taken by the United States is not a violation of GATT. I might say that we support the price of butter and we prohibit the importation of butter from the United States, which is legitimate under GATT, just as it is legitimate for the United States to take any action it likes in connection with oats.

The manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Chairman, has commented on this matter I think is indicative of an attitude which should be condemned in this house. The fact is that the Canadian government has been anxious apparently to be the apologist for the actions of the United States in seeking restrictions on the export of Canadian oats to the United States. There is not one thing that the minister has said that justifies the imposition by the Canadian government upon Canadian producers of oats of a restriction on the export of their oats to the United States.
The fact remains that the Canadian government came to the rescue of the United States government in what would have been an embarrassing situation in relation to our trading relations with the United States, and

relieved the United States government of that particular embarrassment by itself manacling the Canadian producers and exporters of oats.
The story does not end there, unhappily. We see in Washington today that the same kind of pressure is being exercised now in search of restrictions upon the export of Canadian lead and zinc to the United States. I have asked the minister in the house on several different occasions about this matter, and the minister has indicated there have been no communications passing on this subject between the two governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Chairman, I did not so indicate. If I did, it is entirely erroneous. Of course, we have made representations.

I have not looked at the particular statement the minister made but the inference I drew from the statement he made with respect to the question was that there had been no formal communications on this subject in regard to the request that has been mentioned in the press statement from Washington, seeking on the part of the Canadian government some restrictions upon the export of Canadian lead and zinc to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I assure the hon. member that, in the first place, no such request has been received from the United States asking that we restrict exports of lead and zinc. The report of the tariff commission is before the president, and its contents are unknown. Certainly Canada has filed a formal protest against any action that will restrict shipments of Canadian lead and zinc into that market.

I am sure we are glad to hear that because this matter is of very serious concern to the Canadian metal producers. I may say that the press has carried some disturbing reports in this field. For instance, on April 19 a Canadian Press report from Washington read as follows:
The United States likely will ask Canada shortly to curb shipments of lead and zinc into the American market. The request may take the form of a suggestion that Canada volunteer to reduce exports, just as it agreed earlier this year to reduce shipments of oats, United States informants said yesterday.
Canadian exports of lead and zinc to the United States totalled almost $100 million in 1952. The United States domestic industry, faced with declining market, has appealed for some form of tariff protection.
There is another form of restriction that seems to be proposed by Washington at the expense of Canadian producers, which I believe should give us concern. We have seen following these bumper crops of wheat

in this country a vast accumulation of wheat in Canada. I have mentioned already the fact that the efforts on the part of the Canadian government to dispose of that huge surplus in the United Kingdom have not been adequate. Whatever may be said about the proportion or percentage of Canadian wheat out of the total that has been going into the United Kingdom market, the fact of the matter is that for the first 9J months of the present crop year just 196 million bushels of Canadian wheat went into the United Kingdom market, whereas in the full crop year 1952-53 our exports to the United Kingdom amounted to 378 million bushels. It is evident, therefore, there is a drastic reduction in the volume of Canadian wheat exports to the United Kingdom. In the face of that, Mr. Chairman, listen to this. This is a report from Washington dated April 23, and reads:
Ezra Taft Benson says, In friendly spirit, that he would like to see Canada impose controls on her grain, production.
It will be recognized that the gentleman in question is the United States secretary of agriculture, and in making the statement he did he is no doubt reflecting the policy of the United States administration. He added, and we are told he added with a smile:
It would please us if Canada imposed controls on her acreage.
I think this house would like to know whether the Canadian government is going to entertain proposals of that kind from the United States or whether the Canadian government is determined to follow policies that will assure for the Canadian producer markets for his production. What is the Canadian government doing about these matters? Have there been any protests against comments of this kind as to United States' governmental policy?
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have time for only one brief comment on GATT as such. I have made my comments on what I think are disturbing aspects of the attitude of the United States congress towards its responsibilities under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. But what of GATT in the wider context? On October 15 next the nations who are signatories to GATT will be convening for the purpose of planning for the extension of GATT. Since the general agreement was extended at the last meeting, there have been certain developments that have not been commented upon by the minister.
In the first place, there were some changes made at that time in regard to the provisions of GATT. Recognition was given to the fact that the government of The Netherlands was quite justified in applying certain restrictions
Supply-Trade and Commerce upon the importation of certain materials from the United States in retaliation for the imposition of restrictions upon the importation of Netherlands dairy products into that country. Since this matter became a lively subject of concern to us no one in this house so far as I am aware proposed that retaliatory measures be applied against the United States. But I believe we want to know, and we have not been told, whether the Canadian government has now acquiesced in and accepted the breaches of GATT on the part of the United States congress. It was just over a year ago that this house unanimously passed my motion calling upon the Prime Minister who was then about to leave for a conference in Washington to register with the United States government the strong protest of this house against the breaches by the American congress of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, which affected The Netherlands, which affected us and which affected other nations that export dairy products.
We have not heard anything from the government now for over a year as to any protest or any efforts that they are making to seek a removal of those measures taken by the United States congress which are directed against Canadian dairy products, and which are a direct violation of the provisions of GATT. What is the government's policy on this matter? What is the government's aim, and above all what are the government's efforts in this direction, if any?
I close with this question: What do we consider to be the function of government in this country in relation to trade? We are thinking, of course, particularly about external trade, having regard to the jurisdiction of parliament in relation to trade and commerce under the British North America Act.
So far as the Canadian government is directly involved in the sale of any particular commodity, as in the case of wheat, we of course expect of the government that it shall be an energetic and resourceful salesman, having due regard to the fact that the interests of the western wheat farmer particularly are at stake, and that those interests are basic to the health of the whole economy of Canada. But in those cases where the government is not directly involved in the bulk trade of commodities, what is the function of government? As I understand it, the function of government, that which has been assigned to the government by statements which have come from the Prime Minister and others in relation to the whole field of economic activity within the country, is to create a healthy climate within which free enterprise, the enterprise of individuals, may flourish.
