What is the government doing in relation to its duty to create as healthy a climate as may be possible within which individual enterprise and individual salesmanship may flourish? I have drawn attention to certain matters to which the government it seems to me is simply directing a blind eye, and is not even admitting the existence of the problem. And when the government does not even admit the existence of the problem, there is small hope for its addressing its most resolute efforts to the solution of that problem. That is the first point.
Then, in the second place there is this question of Canada's competitive position in the markets of the world. Surely it disturbed, even if it did not surprise, hon. members when they heard the minister say today in his closing remarks-if I heard him correctly-that there was no cause for alarm because Canadian producers at the present time may not be able to compete in certain world markets. Mr. Chairman, surely it must be a matter of concern to each one of us here when the Canadian producer is not in a position to compete with the producers of other countries in the markets of the world. Is this a matter of no concern? Is this a matter of such indifference to us that the Minister of Trade and Commerce can say, "Oh, there is no cause for alarm here", and then sit down and feel perfectly satisfied?
Mr. Chairman, surely that is a poor substitute for facing problems, and facing them squarely. The fact of the matter is-and leading economists in this country have drawn attention to it-that Canada's position in the competitive markets of the world has been placed in jeopardy by a high-cost economy. What is one of the leading ingredients in that high-cost economy? I tell you, sir, it is high government costs and high taxation. It will be remembered-
Time.

Well, nobody pays much attention to what the hon. member for Kootenay East says, with his silly interruptions; and I shall pay no attention to him.
Speaking for the government the Minister of Trade and Commerce said on February 15 that the government had decided that this year would be a year of loosening the purse strings on government spending. Is it any wonder, then, that there is a high-cost economy here, and that that is hamstringing the efforts of Canadian producers to find markets abroad for their produce? It was


in that connection that the Ottawa Citizen, a paper friendly to the government, said this: Bather than respond by giving Canadian manufacturers additional tariff protection, the Canadian government might well consider revising downward its own sales taxes. This would put Canadian business in a better position to compete with American goods, and incidentally with those from Japan and other outside sources. It is true that the lost revenues must be made up. Apart from resort to higher taxes in other fields, the government might find itself taking in more money from taxes at the reduced level, because of the stimulating effect on domestic business.
This government could make a substantial contribution to the improvement of the competitive position of the Canadian producer in the export markets of the world by reducing these impositions that it places upon the cost of Canadian production.
The one thing that would be unforgivable in this situation would be inaction on the part of the government. Inaction results from smug complacency, from satisfaction with the situation as it is, from closing one's eyes to the dangers of the situation, particularly the dangers confronting the Canadian agricultural producer. What we demand is recognition of these difficulties; no Pollyanna attitude, but rather a frank and realistic appreciation of the difficulties and then a determination to grapple with them and, as it is within the government's power, to clean house and in its own way contribute to improving the competitive position of the Canadian producer in the markets of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not speak at great length. I have been particularly interested in the debate which has taken place thus far. While in the restaurant at the noon recess I noted that General Gruenther, commander of the NATO forces, is in Ottawa. I hope he will have a pleasant visit. I think, too, that he might find a concrete method of strengthening his NATO forces if he would listen to some of the debates taking place in the House of Commons today; I am convinced that the most obvious way to strengthen NATO is for the United States to enlarge the economic as well as the military foundations under the alliance.
Recently there has been a good deal of economic friction between the United States and Canada. I believe people on both sides of the border hope that friction will not continue. There are few Canadians who do not realize how dependent we are upon the United States market. The minister told us this morning that 59 per cent of all our exports go there. But that trade certainly is not one-sided. Last year, we bought $757 million more from the Americans than we

sold to them. And so I suggest the Americans, too, should be interested in the maintenance of cordial trade relations between our two countries.
Many Canadians-and I am one of them- feel that recently in trade matters the Americans have not been treating us exactly as we think they should treat a friendly country. Washington originally inspired the Geneva agreement. I remember well that, quite willingly, this parliament turned its back a few years ago on imperial preferences and entered the Geneva agreement. We did so because we believed that it would lead to freer trade, and, to a certain extent, it has.
Yet while we have made major tariff concessions under the agreement, in the ensuing years the Americans have been most reluctant to proceed with a progressive lowering of tariffs. So far as Canada is concerned, most of the concessions the Americans have made thus far have been on raw materials and semi-processed goods. So far as manufactured goods are concerned, the tariff rates are still practically prohibitive. That fact has put most of our manufacturers in this country in a very difficult position.
Today the United States manufacturer has a home market of roughly 155 million people, and he is protected from outside competition by a very high tariff barrier. Our manufacturers in Canada have a potential market of only about 15 million people and because of the low tariff barriers they have to share that market with the American manufacturers.
I find it very difficult to understand the attitude of American businessmen. On the one hand, in a very generous way, they give away billions of dollars in military and foreign aid. Yet, on the other hand, they refuse to lower their tariff barriers to let the other NATO countries strengthen themselves. The paradox does not seem to make sense. I say that the United States trade policy is threatening the very foundations of the NATO agreement today. If the United States congress does not wake up to the fact soon they may find the alliance crumbling. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will give General Gruenther such a message while he is in Ottawa today. If he really wants to strengthen the alliance, let his country take economic measures, as well as military ones.
I should like to know what United States' businessmen fear. These businessmen always preach the virtues of competition. They are always chiding their neighbours that they lack the great competitive spirit which has made the United States great. Yet, as I see
Supply-Trade and Commerce it, these American businessmen are not practising what they preach. They maintain a very high tariff wall to protect themselves from outside competition. The minute the president or anyone else suggests that the tariff walls should be lowered a little, they scream in agony.
The Geneva agreement originally promised a progressive lowering of tariff barriers. I say that our American friends have not lived up to the spirit of that agreement. For more than six years it has been pretty obvious that the United States has failed to reciprocate to an appreciable extent the concessions which Canada has made under the treaty. What is even more serious, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton, on numerous occasions the United States have actually violated the agreement. The case of dairy products was mentioned. The trade minister says that as far as oats and rye are concerned they did not violate the agreement. Well, as I understand it, they certainly violated the spirit of the agreement. I feel the United States government literally blackmailed the Canadian government into accepting those quota restrictions, and they did so at a time when western Canada was bulging with full granaries of oats and rye. I do not think we should have been forced into such a position.
Obviously there are some congressmen and some senators in the United States who think that the Geneva agreement is just a scrap of paper which they can violate at any time for political reasons. According to newspaper reports, the United States is considering embargo restrictions on lead, zinc and fish products. I must say that I am not entirely satisfied with the assurances the minister gave us this afternoon that these restrictions likely will not take place. If the United States does proceed, once again it will be a violation of the Geneva agreement. Once again large segments of our economy are going to be seriously hurt. Once again the United States is going to use Canadians just as marginal suppliers- taking our materials when there is a scarcity, refusing to take them when they are plentiful. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, when this government must make its position clear as to exactly what it will do, if the United States does proceed with the restrictions that are being mentioned.
If the United States is going to continue to violate GATT Canada should re-examine her whole position under the Geneva agreement. Certainly a treaty is of little use to Canada when the main signatory ignores the major provisions. Therefore, I urge this government to make its position crystal clear in

Supply-Trade and Commerce this debate, as to what it will do if the United States does proceed with an embargo on lead, zinc and fish products. As I see it, the Americans should be told that Canada would be forced to retaliate. Canada would have to take counter-measures. Perhaps those counter-measures should include embargoes or restrictions; perhaps they should include some counterbalancing tariff; perhaps they should even include an export tax on asbestos, nickel, or some other product which the United States must buy from us.
I suggested such a policy last December before the embargo was put on oats. It is not going to help either country to get into a price war. If we get into a price war with the United States I do not suppose there is any way in which we can be the winner. Yet sooner or later Canada is going to have to stop turning the other cheek. This government should point out to the United States, as I see it, that there is frustration in this country, disappointment and even bitterness, because of the United States trade policy. Canada wants to be a friend of the Americans; we have always been one in the past, and we want to be in the future. The United States is not helping that process when they indulge in economic nationalism, as they have done in the past few years.
I should also like to say a few words about trade with iron curtain countries. Personally I feel that the Department of Trade and Commerce has been lax in developing trade with such nations as Russia, China and others. Our trade with those countries is almost negligible. I have a Canadian Press report here of last April which says that exports to Russia in the month of March were $25 as compared with $57 a year ago. Britain, Germany, France and Japan are getting into those world markets, and I am afraid -maybe the minister can show that I am wrong-that Canada is missing the trade boat by not following suit.
Earlier this year the Russian ambassador announced that his country was anxious to buy certain Canadian products. Yet so far Canadian authorities have treated the efforts which the Russian ambassador made with apathy, with indifference, and even ridicule. Only a few weeks ago the Russian embassy gave Canadian exporters a long list of products which they would like to buy from Canada. That list included a number of manufactured products. It included foodstuffs, and particularly, as far as western Canada is concerned, it included wheat. I put a question on the order paper which was answered yesterday. The effect of the question was: What has the Department of Trade and Commerce or the government done to try to

sell grain to Russia since the first of the year? In a nutshell the answer was that two representatives from the Russian embassy had called on the department and obtained price lists, delivery dates and so on. To date, it said, there have been no further developments.
Well, Mr. Chairman, what kind of salesmanship is that? Here we have some officials sitting in an office waiting for orders to come. There is no aggressiveness, no imagination, no particular desire to sell, and no follow-up. If I had salesmen like that in my business at home I would be bankrupt very quickly. Out in the west we have 700 million bushels of wheat sitting in granaries, in elevators, in fields and everywhere else. We have a country which says it is willing to buy some of that wheat, and yet our officials in the department do not even bother to get out of their chairs and go over to the embassy to see why no purchase has been made.
Why have the Russians not bought that wheat? Have our credit terms not been good enough? Is the price too high? Do they lack exchange? Do they want some kind of barter agreement? At least let us find out. 1 do not know what the answer is. Maybe their offer was a phony one. If it was, let the minister tell us why it was phony. But with the vast surplus of grain which we have in western Canada any suggestion of an offer to buy should be thoroughly examined. Trade with the eastern world would be good business. I also believe it would help to promote better relations between the power groups in the eastern world and the western world. I ask this government to leave no stone unturned in trying to develop trade with the east in the same manner as Great Britain is doing. Before this item passes I hope the minister will make some comment on those offers to purchase which have been made to Canada by eastern countries.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up the time of the committee at any great length, but I do feel the Department of Trade and Commerce is a very important one and that upon that department rests probably a greater responsibility than on any other government department. Perhaps that is the reason why the most optimistic member of the cabinet is the head of that department.
I listened with keen interest and not without some concern to the minister's summary of conditions as he saw them and the rather delightful optimism he expressed in regard to the future, despite the fact that we have

had certain signs that our economy is not too healthy, and despite the fact that there has been some decline in the export of our lumber, lead, zinc, copper, iron and other products into our greatest market.
He expressed the view that the future was not as dark as some might think. I hope his optimism will be fully justified as time goes on. No one who has any appreciation of the greatness of this country can be other than a long-term optimist and, in fact, I am always more optimistic when I hear a rather fresh change of viewpoint from western Canada, particularly when I hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, who has just concluded, give some indication that he believes certain changes should be made. The changes the hon. member has advocated are not those which his party has advocated in the past, and they were to the effect that we should take more cognizance of the dangerous situation facing our industrial enterprises at the present time.
The Department of Trade and Commerce handles responsibilities which are vital to our normal prosperity, and indeed vital to our security, because only by sound economic development can we become as strong as we require to be in this ever-changing and troubled world in which we live at this particular time. Whether it is in peace or war our industrial development, as the minister has so ably pointed out today, and the changing economic situation through which we are passing demand that the government adopt certain changes in policy.
I am glad the minister has indicated some change in attitude on the part of the government with regard to policy. I do not intend to make a specific issue of the wheat situation as Mr. Speaker has asked us not to do so, but, as has already been pointed out today, we have a tremendous wheat surplus in Canada and no farmer or businessman in Canada is unaware that we have more unsold wheat today and less likelihood of selling it than at any time since confederation.
There is no farmer in this country who is not aware that we are selling pork to other countries for less than we are selling it to our own consumers in order to get rid of it, and that we have a tremendous surplus of butter. Dairymen are being encouraged to milk more cows, but under the present system the more cows they milk the more they will have to milk the treasury, because the butter is being sold at less than cost and the taxpayer is having to pay both the high price for butter and the subsidy in addition to that.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, there are a great variety of problems facing us in this changing economic situation which demand of us a change in approach. This country has swiftly changed from an agricultural to an industrial country, and to the degree that we developed our industrial independence we strengthened our position during the recent terrible crisis of the second world war. No one knows that better than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who played a very important role in the development of the industries of this country, and no one knows better than he the importance of maintaining what might be termed the industrial independence of this country.
Since that time we have watched the expansion of what might be termed a new industrialization such as has not been known before. It has often been said, Mr. Chairman, that we should buy if we want to sell, and how often have I heard that during the last quarter of a century in this house, especially from some of my friends to the left, and from the few free traders remaining on my right. They too have indicated that if you want to sell wheat you had better buy from the country to which you hope to sell.
In Canada that sounds plausible; it sounds popular to the voters; and it sounds pleasant to the ears of people overseas. But that is not always the rule. It is more popular and plausible than it is factual. The Minister of National Revenue appears to be somewhat in doubt. But he knows very well that even though this country bought $700 million worth more from the United States than we sold to her during last year, there is very little hope of the Minister of Trade and Commerce being able to sell much of the 700 million bushels of wheat to that country.
The fact that we have sold the United States many billions of dollars of goods since the latter part of the late century and over the present half of this century does not mean that now, when we are making a fire sale of pork and selling butter at less than cost, we will be able to sell wheat to the United States, or that the United States will take any of these products. You can buy billions of dollars worth more goods from the United States in future but that will not change the present situation.
On the other hand, the United Kingdom over this same period from the latter half of the past century to this half of the present century has given Canada a favourable trade balance every year, and the fact that we fell down in buying goods from Britain in

Supply

Trade and Commerce any one year did not make any very great difference in the amount of wheat, bacon, pork, or other agricultural products she bought from us. We have bought consistently in the old land down through the years and I will even venture to say, Mr. Chairman, that for nearly 70 years we have sold Britain more goods than we have purchased from her, and if the amount were added up I think it would be found that the United Kingdom has poured between $4 and $5 billion more into the trade channels of this country than we have poured into the United Kingdom.
Yet, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out this afternoon, we consistently put our trade eggs in one basket, and God help Canada if the handle of that basket breaks while someone else is carrying it. We have never at any time in our history been more dependent upon the United States economy than we are at the present time.
Our industrial independence should increase with our national growth, if we are as great as we believe we are. We boast about our great resources and our technical ability in manufacturing and industrial production. We should therefore not allow ourselves to be at the commercial beck and call of the United States. We should not be fixing our rates in Washington; we should not be fixing our tariffs according to the views of the United States; and we should not be on bended knee.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was somewhat critical of the United States. I do not think we need necessarily be critical. I think we should allow the United States to handle their own affairs and we should mind our own business. It is our business to look after Canada's trade, and it is the business of the Department of Trade and Commerce to look after that trade.
But, Mr. Chairman, when it was mentioned a few years ago by the leader of this party, and when it was proposed on different occasions that we should have a British commonwealth conference, that suggestion was scoffed at and cast aside. Despite the fact that others who sat here right at that time more or less scoffed at and ridiculed that suggestion when the leader of this party suggested that we should have convertibility of currency and should encourage it, today the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that we are coming closer to convertibility. Today it was mentioned that the commonwealth offers the best chance for trade. Today it was mentioned by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the United Kingdom has


lowered tariffs more than has any other country and that next were the other British commonwealth countries.
The country that we have been growing more dependent upon throughout the years, the country from which we have been taking more goods-by $700 million last year, as was said by the hon. member for Eglinton this afternoon-than they purchased from us, was the first more or less to break the GATT agreement. As the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre has just said, the GATT agreement more or less replaced, or was more or less taken as the alternative to the British commonwealth agreements. For that reason I know that document was looked upon with a certain amount of doubt by many, but everybody was almost afraid to mention it. It was looked upon and handled almost as carefully as if it had been some sacred document that nobody could even look into too far. It is bound to be good for somebody. It was a kind of gunshot prescription for world trade that nobody in the Department of Trade and Commerce ever could fully explain to us. Evidently nobody in the United States understood it at first; and when they did come to understand it, as soon as they understood it they partially repudiated it. It has done no good for Canada.
Yet hidden behind it some place there may be some good will, something that may do some good. It may have helped to sell a little bit of salmon to Spain. It may have helped to sell a few sardines some place else. But by and large it has been of very little use to us here. It seems to me that if we are going to develop as we should develop, more thought must be given to other lines of trade. In Canada there are many more things to sell than wheat, despite the fact that we have a tremendous surplus of wheat.
When the minister today mentioned the Randall report I could not help thinking of our historic dependence upon the United States of America. There are those who deliberately say there is no difference in party policy. Down through the years there has been a difference in party policy. Those who sat to your right, Mr. Chairman, have long since felt that because we live beside this great republic, this great and wealthy nation to the south of us, this most powerful industrial machine in the world, we must dance to their tune, rise with their prosperity and fall with their depression. That policy has been followed by my more or less senior colleagues across the floor who have been sitting here for many years. I know they say little except to themselves, but I know these gentlemen realize very well-or if they do not, their fathers do-what happened when their

party proposed commercial union with the United States of America back in 1887. They have not changed a great deal since then because the year before last we were doing almost two-thirds of our total trade with the United States of America.
We are not following the example of that country which is coming back faster than is any other country in the world. I speak subject to correction with regard to the figure, but I think it is either 27 per cent or 31 per cent of their trade that is with any one country. They have spread their trade all over the world. They were too smart to put all their eggs in one basket.
Again I say this as to countries that buy our resources. They buy them because they need them. They buy our iron ore because their iron ore deposits are failing. They buy our pulp and paper products because their forests have been depleted to a great extent. They do not buy our pork, even when we have to have a fire sale of it. They do not buy our butter when we are up to our ears in butter. They do not buy our grain when we have more grain than we have ever had before in our lives. They produce products of the same type as those that are produced in Canada. Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the hour is rapidly approaching when we shall be in difficulty if we are going to follow that old popular appeal that has been hurled at us so often, namely, that in order to sell you must buy. This has not been proven to be the case down through the years because from the country to which we have sold the most, we have bought the least; and with the country from which we have bought the most we have had the most unfavourable trade balances.
Today the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that we have had a tremendous expansion. We all agree. He stated that the United Kingdom removed more tariff restrictions against us than did any other country. Yet we had a favourable trade balance with her. New Zealand and Australia were more or less next. Mr. Chairman, their relationship is another indication that the commonwealth was never more vital than it is today. As convertibility is now coming on the horizon, as the minister has said, I suggest that a British commonwealth conference would probably be more acceptable now when this government needs to do something. I suggest that it is perhaps not too late to try to restore our position in the British market. The strengthening of United Kingdom and the British commonwealth relationships with Canada is of most vital importance and it promises the greatest outlet for our future.
The minister described how he has turned toward multilateral trade and mentioned that
Supply-Trade and Commerce the GATT agreement expires in 1955. I am not going to go into that matter to any extent except to say that if Canada is going to have a place for all her vast industrial expansion, in order to assist the minister and the Department of Trade and Commerce, the one thing this country needs more than another is a general overhauling, a general research campaign, a general remodelling, revamping and readjustment of our whole tariff structure and our taxation structure in this country.
When you look at the taxation that is raising the costs of our production, you can then see the reason why the textile industries are going out of business in this country. You can see why heavy machinery is coming in here from Japan, West Germany and other places. Mr. Chairman, if you are going to maintain the high standard of living we have in Canada and pay our men for their toil three times as much money as is paid to others, then you cannot buy the things of those who are producing at that much less cost.
I can at least personally be somewhat in agreement with what has been mentioned by some of the Liberal members who ran their election campaign as free traders but who now scream for some change in fiscal policy in order to keep their industries from closing up in North and South Waterloo and in other places throughout this country. Mr. Chairman, there is no chance of our building up our hopes on an economy that is so false as to do nothing but expand the plants themselves and then, when we open the doors for the production of those plants, to say "We will buy the goods where we can buy them most cheaply", because we are following a free trade policy that is afraid to move until the harm is done.
I do not claim that any form of high protection alone is the answer any more than the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre did this afternoon when he hinted that there is a change of heart in his group. I am not sure whether it is a change of heart or a change of hearts, but in any event it is a change of public thinking. It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that with all our great resources we will have a sale for iron ore to those who need ore, we will have a sale for Canada's No. 1 hard wheat to those who cannot buy that type and quality of wheat at any lower price. What the minister said yesterday-and some may be critical of him in this regard-is not what he said some time ago. I am glad he is a smart enough businessman to change because it is not long ago that he and his colleagues said they would not take less than $2.50 a bushel. Now he says we will sell at whatever price we have to take.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Those who sit to your right, Mr. Chairman, would never doubt the Toronto Star, and I read in it this morning that the United States of America may establish a price of $1.55 because they want to test the international wheat agreement. If they drop to $1.55 and the signatories to the agreement refuse to take wheat at that price the agreement will collapse. Then what? Then it will take some smart businessman like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to catch up to the parade and sell, as he said the other day, where people will buy. He will sell at similar prices for similar grades. The old law of supply and demand has been cruel and hard down through the years.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think perhaps the hon. member will not object if I interrupt to say that I think he and others have adhered very well during today's debate to our tacit agreement to which it has been rather difficult to adhere, but I do not think he will mind me saying at this time that if on this item he should make critical remarks with respect to the sale of wheat others will perhaps feel that they should follow suit and others will feel that they should reply. I am sure the hon. member was merely using wheat as one example in his criticism of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but may I suggest that it would assist all of us in this rather difficult position if he would choose another example. I may tell the committee frankly that I have no desire, if I can help it, to be forced into making a ruling today because if I have to then of course we will have to enforce it, and I think we can get along better by consent than by a ruling.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly bow to your ruling. I would not want to set any bad examples or dangerous precedents in the house, which follows the rules so diligently and strangely at times. But I do feel that in this ever-changing pattern, to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred this morning, there is one other item we should not forget. We should not forget the greatest market of all, one that is not very often mentioned in the house, the one that is the most stable, the one that is the soundest, the one that we can depend on most and the only one we control, the home market. If you can keep men employed so that they are able to buy the products of the soil and are able to live well and happily in their homes you will keep the home market going.
The minister has told us today that the outlook for the export of industrial products is not too bright. Our imports are not quite as large as they were last year but they


were very heavy last year. Therefore while the outlook for the export of our manufactured products is not too bright, competition for imports is ever keener and stronger. Oh, how the government lectures industry on cutting costs and improving efficiency. They certainly should be good advisers because there is no institution in all of Canada that knows more about high costs than the government does.
We have spent money faster than at any other time on civilian affairs and, indeed, by all the signs we seem to have got less for what we have spent on military affairs than at any other time. We have spent more for military purposes in the last three years than we spent even during the war. But, Mr. Chairman, it has often been a pastime for those who think it is popular to tell industry how it should operate. I represent a riding that has very little industry. It is mostly agricultural. The industrial people of this country, the manufacturers, have been more or less whipping boys for the politicians since confederation.
I sometimes wonder if we ever pause to realize that today the industrial enterprises of this country are only handling half of their proceeds because with the very high rate of income tax today the government is a powerful silent partner that has taken more than 50 per cent of their total net proceeds every year until lately and is still taking about 50 per cent. Therefore it is not possible to pad any books as some suspicious politicians may have thought was done in years past. The income tax branch is on the watch. They watch the money coming in to a far greater extent than they watch the money going out. They have watched it very carefully. There is no camouflage in that regard whatsoever.
Yet at the same time the industrial companies of Canada are only making an average of 4 to ii per cent. I certainly do not want to be a pessimist. I am not preaching blue ruin. I am not trying to contrast what I think are the economic realities with the delightful optimism of the minister. But I do suggest that there are many signs to indicate that the government should revamp its whole tax structure and reorganize and readjust our tariff structure as well if we are going to make the vast industries that have been built in the last two or three years, and about which we have been bragging, sound operating plants that will give employment to the thousands and thousands of people who are today unemployed and the

thousands more we should have in this country through immigration. If we had sound fiscal policies we could develop that greatest of all markets, the home market.
I do not mean for a moment that the home market will consume all of that product you will not let me talk about, Mr. Chairman, but it will consume a great deal. It will consume a great deal of the butter that the government does not know what to do with. It will consume a lot of the pork that we are selling at fire-sale prices and it will give employment to many more people than are employed at the present time. We have a great industrial structure built up and yet at the same time the products that it is intended to produce are entering this country at a greater rate than they have for many years.
I am not going to delay the item any further except to say once again that I believe it is unfortunate that this young *country, at a time when we are boasting about our greatest growth and prosperity, is increasing its dependence on the United States of America instead of decreasing it. Again I want to emphasize that our objective should be as great a degree of industrial independence as any country of our population can have, for no similar number of *>eople in the world enjoy such resources as ive have. As the minister has so well said, ;ve have iron ore, minerals of all kinds, oil in western Canada in an almost immeasurable amount. The richness of this country is a heritage of which every citizen is proud. Despite GATT, despite our international relationships, I believe it was never more important, in view of the dangerous signs we see on the horizon, for us to have that degree of industrial independence which will create economic safety and, indeed, eventually military safety. I believe that Canada must look after her own business. I know there are many things we can buy from these other countries and there are many of our products they must always buy from us, but I do believe-and it is not an old-fashioned idea but the most progressive and advanced idea that Canada has ever had- that our own resources must be developed by our own people.

I do not know whether or not the minister is enjoying this little session this afternoon. Perhaps if he has his staff there he might answer one question I should like to ask concerning the department. It has to do with the reported sale of some nine million pounds of canned pork to Russia recently. So far as we can get the story from 83276-366
Supply-Trade and Commerce the answers of the department, this pork was purchased at the time the foot-and-mouth disease embargo was imposed. Some of this pork was stored for a while, and then later canned under orders of the government and paid for by the government at a cost of between 50 cents and 60 cents per pound. Later on the government called for tenders on this pork and it was sold at something less than 17 cents per pound. Almost immediately a market was found in Russia by the private enterprise firm, I believe in this case it was Canada Packers. What price they received is not known, and I do not suppose the departmental records would indicate that. I should like to know, and I believe the people of Canada would like to know, why it was that the agents of the department were unable to find that market for Canadian canned pork.
While the minister's staff is looking up the answer to that question perhaps I might make a few general remarks concerning the administration of the department. The people of Canada recognize that in peacetime the Department of Trade and Commerce is the most important department so far as their welfare and prosperity are concerned. We cannot hope to so live within our own borders that we are going to become prosperous by taking in our own washing. The extent to which Canada is able to exchange her surplus goods with other countries, and the extent to which we can economically use our goods within our own borders, will determine the extent to which we are able to keep our factories busy, keep the men employed in the mines, the forests and in agriculture. The policies of the Department of Trade and Commerce decide the prosperity of Canada.
The minister's report today was not one to give the Canadian people a great deal of hope that the prosperity of which we heard so much twelve months ago is going to be maintained. Our record with regard to the fishermen on both coasts, the coal workers in the maritimes, the textile workers, the farm machinery workers, the automobile workers and now the agriculturists on the prairies makes the outlook rather grim. The figures for unemployment are rising in an alarming manner. What is the hope for the people of Canada in this situation? What can we give to these people in the way of hope? They are looking to this superman from the Department of Trade and Commerce, a man whose ability is recognized all across Canada as well as in other countries, to solve their difficult problems.
Yesterday he told us that we must remember we are living in a competitive world. We

Supply-Trade and Commerce must face the facts of life. When he gave us the figures upon which we are to base our hope for prosperity, our hope for trade, really the foundation was revealed to be rather flimsy. Why is it that we always get into this trouble in this competitive world in times of peace? Is it because there is no competition in time of war? Is it because in wartime we can let cost-plus contracts to those who can get them? There is no competition at all in cost-plus contracts. You can employ labour at whatever price you wish because it is paid for under the contract. As soon as we get out of a war episode, a period of war, we have Canada drifting back along with other countries into a period of recession, depression, unemployment, with factories closing and lower prices.
The agricultural workers in the United States have got their government to give them some form of protection against the trouble which may occur when they try to sell their surplus products. In so far as Canada is concerned the agricultural producers must bear the strain of whatever price the government is going to get for their commodities. If there is a price war, then down goes the price, and where it goes to is apparently no concern of the government. They have already stated their policy on more than one occasion in this house, and very emphatically, that they intend to do nothing about giving agricultural producers advances on their production.
The job of the farmer is to produce, and he is doing that job. With the help of nature, with good times and with some return for his work, he is able to solve the problem of production. But you cannot expect him to solve the problem of selling that commodity. He is entirely dependent upon the policies of the cabinet and the administration of this department. When world trade and when Canada's trade in the world is maintained at a high level, we can find markets for our products by sending our people out into the world. If we do that well, then the agriculturists will prosper. If we do not, then he is at the mercy of a price war or any other economic circumstance which may occur.
In the competitive world of today Canada finds herself in a rather difficult position. Our high-priced economy, brought about by high prices during the war and the prosperity we enjoyed during the war, has left us in a difficult position when we have to place our goods alongside the goods of other countries. If we cannot place our goods alongside the other goods at similar prices, then we have to accept lower prices or the goods will not be sold.
The minister's statement today was a surprising statement, and one which I believe
[Mr. Castleden.1

marks a change in his attitude. No longer is there the optimism that everything is all right; we are just as well off as we were last year and we are up over the ten-year average. We did not hear the old statement that when the ice goes out of the lake everything will be all right. Now he says it is not the Department of Trade and Commerce or this parliament that will decide. We must depend on the constructive leadership in the United States. If the commercial policy is favourable, we can go forward with hope. If it is not, it will be difficult to look forward with any degree of optimism.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: May I point out, Mr. Chairman, that I was talking about GATT when I said that. The lack of optimism was about the future of GATT, it was not about the future of Canada. I hope my hon. friend is not trying to distort my words.

No, I am glad to have that from the minister. It is our relationship to GATT upon which, to a large extent, depends Canada's ability to establish any degree of prosperity. The minister admits our economy is slowing down. He maintains that our slowing down is much less than the slowing down in the United States. I am not going to argue the matter with him, but I believe the figures of unemployment in Canada show that we have a greater degree of unemployment, relative to our population, than they have in the United States. Since when have we become so dependent upon the United States, that big giant neighbour which serves this continent with us? Is that the only constructive hope we have? Are the markets of the world to be closed to us; are those markets closed because of our high-priced economy, and because the goods Canada offers are priced pretty much along the same line and at about the same level as those of the United States?
If we are going to depend upon United States prices, then I say the future of the Canadian agricultural producer is very dim, indeed. I say that because we have exactly the same kind of agricultural surpluses they have. Even with GATT they are not looking out for the Canadian producer; they are looking out for themselves. And thus far, at home, they have looked after themselves very well.
If we are going to have to depend upon the consideration our neighbour to the south will give to our producers, then I say things look very dark indeed. The minister says Canada must recognize that she lives in a competitive world. In this competitive world we find ourselves caught; we are left out in the cold because of a price structure and a cost of living that has priced us completely

outside the world's competitive markets. How are we going to get back into those markets? That is the problem facing the minister, and it is a difficult one.
The problem confronting the Canadian government at this time is that of proving that in a competitive world Canada can hold her place, that in a competitive world Canada can provide prosperity for her people in times of peace. And that is the only time we have competition. This objective has not yet been achieved, to any appreciable extent. We knew prosperity shortly after the first war, after 1918. We knew the depths of depression and unemployment prior to 1940. We knew prosperity throughout the second world war and during the episode in Korea. But just as soon as we got out of that we found ourselves faced with an economic crisis.
How long are the people of Canada going to look at the economic problems facing this country and say that we must continue to live in a world which will condemn us in times of peace to a state of depression and want? Surely the choice of the Canadian people must not be between that of having war and prosperity on the one hand or, on the other, peace with unemployment and depression.
The challenge which faces the government, and particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is to prove that the economy under which we live is one which can provide the Canadian people with prosperity in time of peace, so that they may have proper returns for their labour, as well as the right to work and the right to build their homes under natural conditions such as prevail in a competitive economy of this kind.
If this challenge is met, Canada will be pleased, and the members of this group will be pleased. I am sure that in this group there are very few who think the minister can do it. If he can, then we will welcome it as a sign of great achievement. If he cannot, and if conditions continue on the downgrade in the next few years as they have in the last twelve months, those people who have been forced to swallow the medicine of this competitive world will be rising in their places throughout the country and demanding something better.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I have been asked a question which might better have been asked of my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, because the actual plan for the disposal and handling of the pork throughout the period in question was carried out by the agricultural prices support board, which reports to the Minister of Agriculture. However, the facts of the pork 83276-366J
Supply-Trade and Commerce situation are well known. We had in western Canada an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, and because of the foot-and-mouth disease there was an automatic embargo on the part of the United States, on the part of several South American countries who normally offer a market for our canned meats, and on the part of certain European markets.
We were surplus producers of pork, and the government believed that the producers of pork should not be called upon to bear the brunt of the damage resulting from the outbreak of that disease. Therefore it undertook to buy the surplus pork at a floor price which, in my opinion, was very generous indeed. It was the full equivalent of the price at which pork was selling at the time of the outbreak of the disease. That pork was bought. Of course, it took only a short time to fill all the storage space we had; and then it became a question of what to do with the pork.
I am sure my hon. friend would not suggest that we bury it; he would not suggest that we build new cold storage plants in which to store it. We took what we thought to be the only practical way of preserving the food value of the pork, and that was by putting it in cans. I may say that no one was under any illusions that we were going to recover the full cost of that pork after it had been canned. Pork that is canned is not the choice cuts. They are the parts of the animal that are not readily saleable as fresh cuts. Therefore they bring a lower price than could be had when the entire animal was being put in cans.
We canned that pork, and I think my hon. friend was perfectly correct when he said that it cost about 65 cents a pound when canned. Then we had the problem of getting rid of it. We put it on the Canadian market- I believe it was put on at about 35 cents a pound, which seemed to be the price which would be attractive to the Canadian buyer. We sold all we could in that market over a period of about two years. We offered it in other countries at a price no lower than the price at which it was selling in Canada, and we were able to move the bulk of it.
But expert opinion was that it was not safe against spoilage for a period longer than two years. As a matter of fact on inspection it was found that the odd can was beginning to turn colour. At that stage it became a disposal problem, not a marketing problem. Tenders were called for the pork, and bids were received from a number of firms in Canada and outside Canada. The remaining pork was sold to the highest bidder, which happened to be Canada Packers. The sale
5786	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce was outright, with only one provision, that the pork should be sold off the North American continent, because we did not wish to become involved in any dumping problem with the United States, which has very strict laws against the dumping of agriculture products.
After a considerable interval Canada Packers were able to find a market for the pork in Russia. I think they had bids from other European countries, but the bid from Russia was the highest they received. They sold their pork to the Russians. Of course, the government had no interest in the latter phase of the transaction. It had disposed of its ownership of the pork by public auction to Canada Packers.
Were the minister's agents asked to sell this pork, or was it done through the Department of Agriculture?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We were looking for markets abroad throughout the period and we did arrange sales of pork outside Canada from time to time. But when the disposal problem became immediate, all the pork remaining was put up at auction with the concurrence of my officers. We believed that the possibilities of marketing as an edible product in small lots had come to an end, and therefore it was a disposal problem when the remaining pork was put up at auction.
Has the minister the figures for the total amount that was canned?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I do not know.

I am a little hesitant about getting into this discussion on the United Kingdom markets after the very fine speeches by the hon. members for Eglinton and Dufferin-Simcoe, but I feel I must say a few words and try to relate this loss to the maritime economy. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, you can sit back and relax because there is very little danger of my mentioning the word "wheat" in my remarks. Somebody has said that 1953 and 1954 will be the most critical years in our foreign trade since the days of confederation. With that I agree entirely. As we move into our position as the third greatest trading nation in the world we are developing closer ties with the United States and looser ties with the United Kingdom. I do not know where the expression "to put all your eggs in one basket" came from. I imagine it has a Canadian origin; it goes back to at least last year when the minister mentioned it in the estimates. We have never caught on to that expression down in the maritimes. We simply refer to this change


that has come into our trading world as the loss of our traditional United Kingdom markets.
I do not want this to be considered as a plea, Mr. Chairman, or even an attack on the department. I simply wish to point out that our position and our economy today in the maritimes are in very serious trouble because of the loss of the United Kingdom traditional markets. It has been very well dealt with by the hon. member for Eglinton. I would just give one quotation to cover the picture.
I am quoting from the U.S. News and World Report of December 11, 1953. This is a special article on the trade of our nation with the United States and the United Kingdom. They point out that Canada's trade is shifting, and they say:
Back in 1935-39, the U.S. and Britain used to buy about the same amount of goods from Canada. Today, the U.S. outbuys Britain nearly 4 to 1. As a result, Canada now looks to the U.S. for about 60 per cent of its export market and about three-fourths of its foreign supplies.
It goes on to say:
So, on trade, Canada is running a deficit of about a billion a year in its dealings with its big southern neighbour. Close ties with the U.S. can be a problem, as well as a benefit.
There is no doubt that today in Canada we have an unfavourable balance of trade. While there are some serious worries over this condition in the future, I think that at the present time things are not too bad. Certainly central Canada is benefiting to a great degree from traffic across the border, from this north-south condition, but we in the maritimes do feel this loss that I have referred to. It is not a case of the sentiment that we might have for the traditional markets; it is simply that our economy has been completely distorted and wrecked owing to the fact that we have no outlet for our primary produce, and also to the fact that our ports of Saint John-and I think I can speak for Halifax -really miss this United Kingdom and to some extent European trade.
The national harbours board figures which were released a short time ago showed that in 1953 the ports of Halifax and Saint John were the only ports in Canada which showed decreases in tonnage figures. It is not difficult to follow along from there and show that most of the tonnage to go through our ports is traffic and trade with the United Kingdom and to a small degree with Europe. That is the situation, Mr. Chairman, and I am calling it to the attention of the minister to show him that our problems are very serious down east in that respect.
Various changes could be referred to in our relations with the United States. I will not

spend too much time on them, but the United States has already flouted or perhaps misused or taken advantage of the escape clauses in the GATT agreement. Import restrictions have been placed on various commodities by the United States, and we shall probably hear of more in the future. There is the worry that a trade recession will hit the United States to a much greater degree than other countries, and of course we shall feel the loss first in that respect. We also have the problem of dumping here which of course is tied in with our trade with the United States.
I could refer generally to a recession that might affect the economy of the United States. Recently they have felt perhaps a slight recession, more so than we have. Unemployment was every bit as bad over there, if not worse, than in Canada this past year. Their textile industry is in the same dire straits as ours is, and generally speaking there has been a recession in the United States that is much more noticeable than here. We are tying ourselves to their economy in a very dangerous fashion when we count on them for so much of our export and import trade.
There is no reason why we should be tied to the United States. We can go back in history to 1911 and previous times and we shall find that it has been quite a political issue. I refer to this tie and relationship that we have with our friends across the border. Very few valid reasons could be given for being tied up in this way.
I simply suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we have our difficulties in the maritimes over the loss of our markets. It is really serious. I could not help thinking the other night when the minister referred to an Ontario member. He referred to him as my hon. friend down east. I do not think that is in keeping with our traditions, to refer to anybody in central Canada as an easterner. The minister has certain interests in the maritimes and always has had. When he is down on his well-deserved holiday at St. Andrews this summer he might take a day off and come up around Saint John and I am sure that inquiries will convince him that we are really feeling the pinch in our economy over the loss of our traditional United Kingdom markets.
I should like to close with this quotation from the Canadian Chartered Accountant of March, 1954, at page 146:
Canada today is facing some crucial decisions with regard to her foreign trade pattern. Based on our recent experiences, it is apparent that new fundamental policies are in order. Our present
Supply-Trade and Commerce pattern is one in which two-thirds of our foreign trade is transacted with one country whose reliability as a stable market is far from assured. The year 1954 promises to be a year for bold decision, requiring all of us to reorientate our thinking in accordance with the economic realities of the age.

Ever since I came to parliament in 1940 the minister has been doing a great job. During the war years he earned the title of the czar of his country. I just made a note of some of the responsibilities he had during the war: aircraft production, synthetic rubber, shipbuilding, steel, lumber, cement, T.C.A., radio, and housing. He had the good fortune to have a blank cheque and members in all sections of the country are agreed that the money was not squandered, and the department of munitions and supply played a very important role in the winning of the war. However, I have a feeling that the minister's role for the next few years is not going to be so easy. Just as his was the responsible portfolio during the war, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will have to take the major responsibility for the government in seeing that a high level of employment is maintained in Canada, and a maximum volume of trade and commerce.
I will mention merely a few of the industries which are now causing concern. We have had delegations in Ottawa during the life of the present session, from the textile industry, the farm machinery industry, the automobile industry, and from agriculture. These represent important sectors of our Canadian economy. The illness of one not only affects the health of the others, but that illness affects every Canadian, and the representations made by the spokesmen for these four groups I have mentioned would indicate that their problems require immediate attention.
I am more particularly concerned naturally with the problem of agriculture and I am afraid I cannot go along with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe who suggested we had good times when his party was in office. The minister gave us some figures last night which went back for a number of years. But from his department this morning I also received some figures which indicate the amount of the national income which has gone to agriculture over a period of years.
I will go back to 1926 which is the best year the farmers ever had, when 14-8 per cent of the national income went to agriculture. Just under 20 per cent of the Canadian people come within the category of farmers so in the good old twenties 20 per cent of the people had 14-8 per cent of the national

Supply-Trade and Commerce income. The farmers took their worst beating during the depression and in 1931 then-share of the national income went down to 2-9 per cent. In 1932 it was a little better when they received 4-1 per cent, and in 1933 they received 3 per cent. During the war years the farmers got up to 12 per cent and it was 12-1 in 1944. It dropped after that but in 1948 it again went up to 12-1 per cent. In 1951 it rose to 12-3 per cent, and last year, 1953 it went down to 8 [DOT] 8 per cent.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think that when just under 20 per cent of the people are getting about 8 per cent of the national income it is the responsibility of their friend and advocate, the minister who is in charge of trade and commerce, to do something to see about getting a better market for their products, or by some means see to it that those who have been regarded as the salt of the earth should have a fair share of our national income.
During the war the minister and the cabinet demonstrated that it was possible to plan our production and consumption with a high level of employment. During the depression years we balanced our production and consumption with a low level of production and lower standards of living every year. During the war the minister was in charge, as I said, of shipbuilding. As I recall it, there was one year when every week a ship was launched and loaded with Canadian goods and was sent to the bottom of the ocean before it reached the other side. In other words, we were just holding our own-the submarines were sinking our shipping at the same rate as we were building and loading our ships.
Yet it seems strange that during that period Canadians were able to use Canadian materials and workmen to build ships, fill them with lumber, wheat and metals and send them out on their way to join in the battle for freedom. Before these ships reached their destination they went to the bottom of the ocean, but in the process we were able to create prosperity for those in the shipbuilding industry and those engaged in the manufacture of the products that went into the ships.
Having been able to do that with a million of our youngest and strongest people in the services it would not seem unreasonable to expect the minister now and somehow to find a formula to solve our difficulties. It would seem that the same people who worked in the shipyards and in the forests should be able to find some constructive work.
Those of us who sit in this part of the house have some theories we think sound. The minister has never advocated these prin-


ciples and has never been elected on a mandate to carry out the policies we would advocate. But he was elected to carry out a mandate to provide full employment and a high standard of living for the Canadian people.
The right hon. gentleman is one of those who demonstrated during the war years that what were hitherto considered to be impossible tasks were very easy tasks to perform, and now that we are facing a crisis, which is in many respects very serious, he has another opportunity to demonstrate his ability. The minister has not publicly admitted that the situation is serious, but it is not going to be very long before we have an increasing number of industries, besides those which I have mentioned, which will be coming to the cabinet to place their case before it.
I have letters here from a number of municipal secretaries in my constituency regarding the position of tax arrears at the end of 1953. I think it is very clear that everyone wishes to pay his taxes as soon as he can and if he can and that is true of every country. Taxes and death are certain in every country. In the Hazel Dell municipality arrears in December were $80,000 compared with $68,000 in 1952; in the Buchanan municipality the arrears were $44,000 in 1953 compared with $32,000 in 1952; in Livingston the arrears were $31,000 compared with $24,000; in Keys the arrears were $47,000 compared with $38,000; in Invermay they were $26,000 compared with $21,000; in Porcupine they were $80,000 compared with $78,000; in Kelvington they were $45,000 compared with $39,000; and in Moose Range they were $97,000 compared with $89,000. These municipalities are located in a part of Saskatchewan where we have never really had a crop failure or poor crops. It is a choice part of the country-
They have good crops and good prices but they do not pay their taxes.

It is not as my hon. friend suggests. The western farmers are not rolling in the lap of luxury. It is true a great many farmers have cars and their position is much better than it was at any time during the thirties; it is no use denying that and I would be the first to admit it. When farmers get 8 per cent of the national income they are in a much better position than when they get 3 per cent, but it is as plain as A B C that when 20 per cent of the people only get 8 per cent of the national income they are not getting as high a standard of living as they should have. That is one of the reasons why you have arrears in taxes.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think the problems of the farmers, the textile workers, the farm machinery workers, and the automobile workers-other hon. members can speak for the fishermen, lumbermen, and coal miners who have problems in a great many parts of Canada-should be dealt with now, and I would suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to have to give some leadership in the cabinet which, apparently, is not facing up to these problems.
May I say just a word about trade with the United Kingdom. As I said previously, I had a short visit in the United Kingdom last fall. I had not previously been aware that the bomb damage done there by the war was as extensive as it was. I feel that we have made a mistake during the years in not accepting a fairer share of the total cost of the war. I think we asked the British, who were exposed to bomb damage and enemy action every night, to carry a share that was greater than their fair share.
I think we must realize that we are living in a very small world. If the British now find it necessary to go into other parts of the world to buy their wheat at a price lower than that which is being offered in Canada, the fact that during the war we sold wheat to Great Britain at a price that appeared to be lower than the world price does not mean that we can now ask that the British standard of living should be driven lower and lower when we are unwilling to accept from the British a larger volume of their goods.
I think the Canadian people must realize that unless we are going to make it possible for more British goods to come into our country, and unless we are going to accept the fact that part of the cost of repairing the war damage in Great Britain is a legitimate cost for the Canadian people to bear, we cannot expect to have as large a volume of Canadian goods going into the British market as we have had going there during past years.
What I have said of Canada is, of course, more applicable to the United States. During two wars our rich and powerful neighbours to the south sat on the sidelines for too long a time. Of course, when they finally came in, their help was an extremely important factor in turning the tide. Nevertheless, there is no doubt about it that at the end of both wars the United States found itself in a much stronger position than it was in at the beginning. For the sake of the free world, I think the United States should be carrying a larger share of the cost of repairing the war damage in Europe and of helping
Supply-Trade and Commerce the people in the underprivileged countries of the world to get a standard of living that is more comparable with that in the United States.
I therefore suggest that the minister act on the proposal made by the hon. member for Assiniboia with respect to trying to negotiate with the United Kingdom with a view to having a larger volume of British goods come into Canada on a basis similar to that on which we bought our rubber or our silk during the war. The Minister of Trade and Commerce bought up large supplies of silk and rubber. Had it not been for his foresight and that of his department, the outcome might have been different. I think it would be quite legitimate now for the minister to set up a board, similar to the one he had then for the purchase of silk or rubber, to purchase these commodities in Great Britain and to supply them through the regular channels in Canada, so that more British goods could be consumed in this country and so that the best customer we have had for so many years should be able to continue to purchase and to use Canadian goods.

I just want to make one observation, Mr. Chairman, with regard to pork. The minister has more or less given the assurance that, under the tender, it was stipulated that the pork would be shipped outside of the North American continent. In the minds of some people there seems to be some doubt whether that stipulation was carried out. I have no very good reason for saying that, except more or less rumours. I wonder whether inquiries could be made in order to satisfy the committee that that agreement was carried out.

To put it in other words, Canada, a member of the British commonwealth of nations, did enter into an agreement with an exporting country, Cuba, for the purpose of increasing trade between the two countries and took a certain amount of sugar from that country. 2.	Canada is the only commonwealth importer of sugar of any consequence outside the United Kingdom.
