speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer the questions about the sugar agreement. The sugar agreement really produces a cartel, if you like. The principal producing countries in the world have formed themselves into a group and signed an agreement. The agreement provides principally that sugar will not be sold below a minimum price of $3.25 per hundred pounds and that it will not be sold at a price above $4.35 per hundred pounds. Sugar is to be sold within that price range, and the agreement provides that acreage shall be reduced in case of surplus or increased in case of shortage.
You ask why Canada signed. I do not quite know why we signed except that our principal trading countries were very anxious that we should. The United Kingdom asked us to support the agreement. Cuba, with whom we had developed a good trade, made a similar request. Before we did so we got an agreement from Cuba in the most explicit terms that the favourable trading conditions that we enjoyed in Cuba as the result of our purchase of Cuban sugar for a three-year period would carry on without that purchase, provided Canada would sign the sugar agreement.
We do not like cartels. We do not like to be members of them. However, there seemed to be no penalty in it and therefore we decided to sign the sugar agreement. Canada is free to buy its sugar from any member of the agreement, which includes practically every sugar producing country that Canada has ever patronized. We can see some advantage in a stable price. The difficulty that our beet sugar producers had in the past resulted from an abnormally low price in the cane producing areas. The fact that there is a cartel among the producers is a protection to our sugar beet growers and the fact that there is a maximum price, which is quite reasonable, is a protection to the consumers of Canada.
Perhaps the effect of the agreement as far as Canada is concerned will be beneficial. There is a penalty with respect to special exclusive agreements being made between a member of the sugar cartel and an outside purchaser. Canada cannot be penalized because there is no way of penalizing Canada under the agreement; but if we made an exclusive arrangement with Cuba, as we did in the three years previous to the agreement, Cuba could be penalized under the terms of the agreement. However, no such agreement has been made.
Our three-year agreement terminated at the first of January of this year and the sugar agreement was signed subsequent to that date. We are a member of the agreement
Supply-Trade and Commerce but we have no special arrangements with anyone. Our refiners buy their raw sugar where they please and make their own arrangements as to price. The government is out of the sugar business, I am happy to say, and I have heard no repercussions from any source on that account. I hope that answers the questions. If there is another question perhaps the hon. member will ask it again.
I should like to ask the minister if in his opinion coffee, as well as sugar, is perhaps handled today by a cartel.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sure the price would not be any higher than it is. If you could stabilize the price of coffee within a reasonable range that might be helpful, but coffee is a more restricted crop. Sugar is grown in a good many countries and is susceptible to sharp increases in acreage and sharp decreases when the plants in an area are diseased. No one has ever suggested a coffee cartel that I know of, and I hope no one ever will, because I do not like cartels and I do not think the people of Canada like cartels or anything about them.
Can the minister tell us what these prices were based on? Were they based on raw sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The prices are for raw sugar f.o.b. Cuba.

I should like to say a few words at this time and in doing so it is not because I feel myself competent or qualified to advise the Minister of Trade and Commerce or anyone else in the house. There are a few matters with which I wish to deal, but I can tell hon. members that I will not make a speech on wheat. Since those in this corner have started to call me Mr. Wheat I thought I would set hon. members' minds at rest at the outset by saying that I am not going to deal with that unmentionable subject at the moment. I just rise to try to keep the record straight on a few things that have been brought up during this discussion. We have listened to some of our friends from Saskatchewan who are not as timid as I am vocally, and yet I feel that in justice to Saskatchewan and a large number of people who live there engaged in this business of providing such a large proportion of our export market with this cereal, which is our only visible means of support, I should like to keep the record straight.
Before doing that, I want to register this comment. At the moment in trade and commerce we are in a period of readjustment throughout the whole world. For a number of

Supply-Trade and Commerce years since the war there has been a great disparity between ourselves and those upon whose areas the battles were fought and a great deal of destruction took place. The standards of living of these people, who suffered most during the war, were brought to a very low level. Naturally, when the people of London and Berlin, as well as other areas, lived in rubble, with no visible means of support, the standard of living was very low. We on this continent, the great industrial machine of the world, were relatively untouched. Immediately after the war there was a period in which we began to supply the wants of those people in order to try to rehabilitate them. The United States gave grants to the work, and so did we.
As soon as the people in those areas began to find their feet, as it were, naturally they went into the business of production. They could produce at a lower figure per hour than we could because their standard of living was low. Even 25 cents or 50 cents an hour looked big to them, and Britain and the rest of these countries that suffered so much are coming back. In this process, we on the North American continent built up for ourselves a very high standard of living. The people engaged in the British electrical industry will work for 53 cents an hour, whereas our people ask $1.53 an hour. Sometimes we wonder why the Britisher gets the contract.
I am not saying anything against a high standard of living; goodness knows, I am one of those who like a high standard. These are the simple facts of the modern world in which we live.
A few moments ago I mentioned that we were in a period of readjustment. I feel that an adjustment will have to be made in one form or another, no matter what we say or do. It is a natural process that is taking place. Those who would place all the responsibility upon this parliament are a little bit "off the beam." We in western Canada should remember that there are farmers in other parts of this country besides Saskatchewan. I sit here amid some who live among farmers. I hear them discuss the fact that they have four thousand barrels of potatoes, and one man says the price of potatoes is really low. When I hear that, I begin to think of the bushels in our granaries out west, 1,000, 2,000 or 3,000 bushels. Before I came down here I had no idea that there were commodities piled up in such quantities as 3,000 or 4,000 bushels of potatoes. The potato growers have their problems, just as we have ours. I am not attempting to speak for them; that is up to them. I may say that all down the line the same thing holds true.


We say that we produce too much of this product that I must not mention this afternoon. However, we produce more textiles than we need; we produce more potatoes than we need; and we produce a lot more of a good many things than we need. As I mentioned in a radio broadcast the last time I was in Saskatchewan, we people in Saskatchewan seem to think that this product I must not mention this afternoon is the largest factor in our trade. If you look at the figures for pulpwood, for example, you will find that there is as much pulpwood that goes into internatonal trade as there is of this particular cereal.
Just to keep the record straight, and because we have had such adjectives as catastrophic used in connection with drawing a picture to illustrate that we, in the province where I was born and raised, are facing economic collapse, I should like to say a few things. In fairness to the other members of parliament here who will be asked from time to time to consider where we in the west fit into the Canadian economic picture, perhaps it would be well to keep the record straight. As you know, there is an international trade fair taking place in Toronto now. At this particular fair Saskatchewan, along with the other provinces, has a booth. In this booth, from which we are trying to establish relationships as a province with the businessmen in other parts of the world, we have a publication entitled "Saskatchewan Invites You". There is a picture on it of a very handsome gentleman whose voice was heard in this house years ago, Mr. T. C. Douglas, the premier of Saskatchewan. I am going to quote from this publication "Saskatchewan Invites You", with the picture of Mr. Douglas on it. The heading is, "Up-to-date Information about Saskatchewan". I am going to read this, but before doing so I may say that I have been digging up some figures just to satisfy myself that things are not perhaps quite as bad as I am being told they are at the moment. However, we are not just as flush as we might be. We have a little dollar shortage-perhaps it is a big one-that arises because we have not sold these two billion bushels we have grown in the last three years. But we are selling some.
Now this is information about Saskatchewan, and it reads as follows:
The average per capita income in Saskatchewan in the past year has been estimated at $1,360 which is again about 12 per cent above the national average.
For the third successive year, Saskatchewan led all provinces in the annual percentage gain of retail sales, increasing 7-2 per cent to an estimated $817 million.
A 15 per cent increase in life insurance sales during the year indicates a parallel advance in personal

savings in Saskatchewan. The value of work performed by the construction industry jumped from $181 million in 1952 to $217 million in 1953. The industry employed 24,000 persons.
Capital investment in plant and machinery advanced from $15-9 million in 1952 to $21 million in 1953.
Investment in exploration and development of oil and natural gas last year reached well over $50 million and this year will approach $70 million. In addition, refinery capacity in the province has more than doubled in recent years. Production of 2-8 million barrels of oil and 1-5 billion cubic feet of natural gas in 1953 may well be doubled in 1954.
Mineral output in the past year was valued at $48 million without including the value of extensive uranium production.
Employment in Saskatchewan has increased about 4 per cent since 1949, compared to a national increase of less than 2 per cent.
That is, for the rest of Canada.
The Saskatchewan wheat crop in 1953 totalled 375 million bushels. This is 13 per cent lower than the record production of 1952, but is 61 per cent higher than the average of the preceding ten years.
Good government out there.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak, and I shall speak only briefly. In order to keep the record straight, as we have been told, there are one or two remarks I should like to make.
First of all, I have not heard any member from Saskatchewan, either in this party or elsewhere, plead poverty on behalf of the farmers of that province. It is true that for the last ten years Saskatchewan has developed tremendously under the leadership of the gentleman who was mentioned by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, the Hon. T. C. Douglas. There is no question whatsoever about it, that the figures placed on record this afternoon are an eloquent tribute to what has been done in that province.
Again, I am not taking anything away from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is in his seat this afternoon. I have very high respect for him, and I know he has done much to further the interests of this country. He has done much in an effort to further some of our trade policies. But I do wish to say this to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, that in the past we have had periods of prosperous years, and in the past those prosperous years have been followed by depressions. When we see farm prices falling, whether they are the prices of wheat, of oats, of milk or of potatoes, they are ominous signs for the economy of this country. We find usually that the first drop indicating anything in the nature of a recession is a drop in farm prices. Other prices then also come down gradually. What we are anxious to do is to see that under those farm commodities there is something of a floor, so that the people in the rural areas may continue to buy the products of the industrial areas. I believe that ultimately we are not going to put the kind of floors under those products that we have been putting under them in past years for a year or so. I believe that sooner or later in large part the policies that have been adopted in a number of other countries in the world, where there are forward prices, where a farmer knows before he puts the grain in the ground what he is really going to get this year and in a couple of years, will be adopted here. When a calf is born on his farm the farmer will know what he is going to get for the finished steer at a minimum price four years from now or three years from now, if it is a three-year-old steer. He will know what he is going to get for eggs and butter over a period of time. That is the policy worked out in a good many countries. That is the policy that
[Mr. Mang.l
has kept production high in agriculture, for example, in the United Kingdom, and that is all we have in mind. We are not denying that the policies of the federal and of the provincial governments have enabled our people in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba producing farm commodities, and in other provinces too, to enjoy a better standard of living than they had in the old cutthroat competition days, when there were no floors and everything went in the direction in which it cared to go.
Under this item we are discussing the policies of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and these things have to be taken into consideration. I merely rose to tell my hon. friend that at the moment there are ominous signs in our economy. It is well that hon. members from various farm constituencies in all parts of Canada should draw the attention of the government to those ominous signs and ask for some protection against them. Let us bear in mind that in the depression years some great corporations and companies in this country did not feel the depression a bit. They were protected. They are in a protected market. The farmers are in an unprotected market, or were before the war. What we want to see is equality. If there is to be a readjustment, as my hon. friend says, then it has to be a readjustment all round. If we have great industries that are enjoying protection and are able to keep up prices by turning labour out into the street in order that they may reduce production and keep prices up, then it is the duty of the government to exercise its power and interfere, and exercise some control.
I am saying to my hon. friend that we are not complaining that our farmers are poverty-stricken. It would not be true if we did. But what we are pointing out is that in the past we have seen periods of prosperity followed by periods of acute recession and depression when the bottom dropped right out of the market-and when the bottom drops out of the agricultural market it drops out of the industrial market.
If there is one lesson we learned during the war it was that in this respect the interests of the workingman in the city and the worker on the farm are identical. In my province, when eggs were selling at 3 cents a dozen a million people were on relief in this country. When wheat was 21 cents a bushel a million people were on relief in this country. In the industrial areas there was no work and no prices for farm products. What we are anxious to see is that steps are taken by the government and by this department to see to it that that kind of thing does not recur in the future. That is all we have in mind.

I am sure we are all gratefully moved by the speech of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I am sure the minister in particular must have been delighted to know that he is a legendary figure not only when the price is going up but when it is coming down. We do not grow very much wheat in Greenwood, and that is all I am going to say about wheat, Mr. Chairman.
I want to make a few remarks, perhaps more in the nature of questions which the minister can answer later. But there was one point of interest that I wanted to put on the record. We all seem to agree that the minister is an optimist. I think he calls himself that, and we often call him that. I thought I would find out what an optimist is and so I looked in the dictionary. A little to my surprise I found-perhaps the minister will be surprised, too, to find what he really is when he describes himself as an optimist- that in the world of business he is associating himself with the philosophers, because I found that the definition of an optimist is a doctrine, a philosophic doctrine, that the actual world is the best of all possible worlds, or the view that good must ultimately prevail over evil in the universe. I am sure it is a great comfort to us all to know that that is the background of the minister's attitude in the things which he does and leaves undone. I bring that forward just as a key perhaps to the explanation of some of the things which we may not fully understand at the moment. We will try to believe that the explanation will come and that when it comes it will have this characterization of great wisdom.
There is of course a danger in optimism, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out. He referred to Nelson's telescope and one might refer also to rose-coloured glasses. As I listened to the minister this morning I had the feeling that some of the favourable features he talked about, however pleasant in themselves, would be more significant at the moment if they seemed to be producing better results.
The minister spoke about the improvement in Europe, and the United Kingdom freeing of trade channels; but actually when we look at what we exported to the United Kingdom last year we find that it is $80 million less, and therefore I feel that, however pleasant it is to know that in certain directions the British are freeing their channels of trade, it is mainly in the sterling area and in the non-sterling countries outside North America, and that at the moment the attitude toward us is not nearly so co-operative.
The minister also referred to South American countries such as Brazil. I made some inquiries about Brazilian exchange but did
Supply-Trade and Commerce not go into it because it is a puzzle that is beyond me. It does seem a fantastic situation that they have there. So far as I can see, it is not going to facilitate us very much in carrying on trade there.
The minister also spoke about convertibility, and here I want to say one word. The Minister of Finance has spoken with optimism about it. When I asked him a question the other day he gave me a not very informative answer. The effect of it was to assure me that he was still regarding it in an optimistic frame of mind. However pleasant it may be for the minister, and the rest of us, it does not take us very far. My own feeling is that convertibility, true convertibility, is much more in the hands of the United States than it is in the hands of the United Kingdom. Actually, my understanding is that at the moment we have in a narrow sense convertibility with the United Kingdom in the sense that whatever they buy they can pay for in dollars; but the answer is that they restrict what they can buy by quotas and embargoes of various sorts, so that their purchases match their available dollars. In that sense you have convertibility of money, but you have a great restriction of trade, as shown by those figures I have just quoted. Therefore, when the minister speaks in rather optimistic terms about convertibility of sterling, I feel just a little uneasy for fear he is not being fully realistic.
The best information I can get from people who I think are well-informed in London is that they do not think the British people are putting convertibility as their top priority. They are able to deal pretty well in a good many other countries of the world, and convertibility of sterling with the dollar involves certain tightening of the belt; it involves certain stringent measures against any kind of inflation. And as I say, the best information I can get leads me to believe that they have not put it as a top priority. I come back again, therefore, to it and say it depends far more on the United States and on the attitude which they are going to take towards trade. Now, the minister was quite realistic about that this morning. I do not think he spoke too optimistically about the immediate situation in the United States. But actually when we turn back to the meeting in March last we find the account of that meeting not very reassuring, and what has happened since is even less reassuring. I have here the Montreal Star for March 17, and the article reads as follows:
Canada and the United States, in a top level inter-cabinet conference ending here today, agreed to consult together on steps to be taken in handling the most pressing issue between the two countries, disposal of excessive stocks of farm products.

Wheat was the principal commodity used as an example in discussing effect of the agreement.
One way to express the results from the Canadian viewpoint, it was suggested, would be to say that, while the United States may tread on our toes, she will give us warning first.
It is not a comforting statement. We have had a good deal of treading on toes, though I am not quite sure how much warning was first given. At any rate, coming back to what the hon. member for Eglinton said this morning, and what he said seemed to me sounded the bell, although the United States is actually very much bigger than we are we do not have to truckle to them, and we can talk to them as man to man, though one just wonders whether we perhaps have been a bit too complacent.
Now I come back to the Montreal Star, with regard to the meeting of March last:
While it provided ground for claiming a victory for Canada, a communique marking the end of the sessions was expected to emphasize that the greatest achievement lay in the fact that the four ranking cabinet members of each of the two countries could sit down together, define their common interests, and find that both countries want to help each other.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have heard it is very pleasant for them to sit down together.
I hope they did it in appropriate circumstances of comfort and refreshment. But it leaves one rather cold when we find out that the practical results are that they found out that both countries wanted to help each other. Now, Mr. Chairman, it is the evidence of that that we want. It is the result which flows from that that we want, and the hon. member for Eglinton this morning had a good deal to say to indicate that the results so far have not been what we would like.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I want to thank the hon. member for looking up the meaning of the word "optimistic". It is a purely altruistic act, because my friend has not an ounce of it in his system, and it is very helpful to know just what it means. I looked up the word "pessimism" which is of particular concern to my hon. friend. The definition is:
Tendency to look at the worst aspect of things; doctrine that this world is the worst possible, or that all things tend to evil.
I deny that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
However, I will take off my rose-coloured glasses. I have this satisfaction, namely that I have gone against public opinion pretty consistently since 1944 and I have never had any tendency to take back any prediction I made during that period. I have heard my hon. friend discuss various subjects and I have never


known him to be right during that entire period, so perhaps we can both be reasonably happy.
My hon. friend is pessimistic about convertibility. Well, I am not. I believe there are tendencies which indicate that it is not far away. It is a complicated subject and no one country can practise it successfully in the European scene without being joined by other countries. That preliminary work is going ahead. The monetary agreement with Germany is a step in that direction, and I think England is better satisfied than previously that their well-being is not so dependent on the prosperity of the United States as they had at first supposed.
I pointed out in the remarks I made that even though there has been some economic setback in the United States in the past few months, Britain's trade position with the United States has continued to improve during that period. However, that is by the way.
My hon. friend belongs to his school of thought and I belong to mine, and I wish I could win him over because his life would be very much happier. But there is no point in undertaking a hopeless task.
However, I would like to say a few words in reply to a number of hon. members who have pointed out that a great deal of our trade is directed toward the United States. I might point out that Canada is a free economy, perhaps the freest economy in the world. Any Canadian citizen is free to buy anywhere he likes in the world, and Canadian currency is convertible to any currency in the world.
In addition, any Canadian citizen is free to sell his goods in any market in the world and the Department of Trade and Commerce is equipped to help him to do so because we are organized in every market in the world.
We make a determined effort to help our people sell their goods in the United States, and we have a strong service there for that purpose. We have an equally strong service in the United Kingdom and anyone with a desire to sell his products in the United Kingdom receives all the assistance the department can give. The same is true of any country you care to name in Europe. We are represented in 50 countries throughout the world by trade commissioners who are capable, well trained, and thoroughly familiar with their market.
That is the function of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is said: "Why not stop selling so much in the United States?" But it is not our job to stop selling so much in the United States. It may be asked: "Why

do we sell in the United States?" It is the handiest market; goods can be delivered at the lowest freight rate compared with any other market in the world; there is no trouble about currency; and theirs is a free economy just as ours is a free economy. It is the most natural thing in the world for anyone who desires to export goods from Canada to examine the possibility of sale in the United States market.
It is because of these facts that a very considerable proportion of our exports are sold in the United States. We know that certain things will not sell in the United States. We cannot sell wheat. Why? Because the United States grows all the wheat that that country needs and has a surplus to export just as we have. There are certain other products we cannot sell in the United States, but we find markets for these products elsewhere.
It is a natural market place, but there should be no reason why things which cannot be sold in the United States should not be sold elsewhere.
It may be asked: "Why do people buy so much from the United States?" It is a voluntary act on their part and I presume the reason why they buy from the United States is that they find they can be better suited by the products sold in that country. Certainly I know of no other reason. There is no inducement put out by the government of Canada to people to buy goods in the United States other than in their own interests.
In the matter of tariffs, the tariffs against United States goods are the tariffs charged against goods from every favoured-nation country. As far as the United Kingdom and the commonwealth are concerned we have preferential tariffs. I have forgotten the proportion of goods which come in from the United Kingdom free of duty-but perhaps I have it here. The goods which came in in 1952 amounted to a total of $359,757,000, and of that amount $202,938,000 entered duty free. That was 56-4 per cent of our total imports from the United Kingdom.
We offer tariff preferences for those who wish to buy their goods in the United Kingdom, as an inducement for them to do so. I do not know how the government could go further, except by erecting prohibitions against purchases in the United States. Assuming for the moment that we agreed with the opposition -and I may say that I do not at all agree with them-that we have too much trade with the United States, the only way in which we can stop it is to put up artificial barriers in the way of prohibitions or to put on excessive duties against the United States, a procedure which is, of course, unthinkable.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I hope that those who weep and complain about the size of our trade with the United States perhaps will, before this debate finishes, tell us just what we should do to re-orient our trade. It is the feeling of the Department of Trade and Commerce that we need every market in the world and that we need to use that market in the best interests of Canada, Canadian business and the Canadian consumer. That is the natural direction of Canada's trade. In a free economy people buy where they like. There is only one way that I know of in which to increase imports from the United Kingdom and that is to have more Canadian citizens take an interest in buying in the United Kingdom, search out things that can be bought there to their better advantage than elsewhere, and direct their purchasing towards the United Kingdom. That is the only answer I can give. I am exceedingly tired of having opposition members, who have no responsibility in the matter, stand up, denounce the United States as an octopus and say that we should not have so much trade with the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a few moments, but I do not think these opportunities should pass without someone from my province making some comment upon the trade treaties which have just been signed between Canada and Portugal, Spain and now Italy. For many years in Newfoundland our salt codfish industry was a continual worry to us. This market we were losing year by year. So much was that the case that many people felt that it was a hopeless position we were being placed in and that we could never get it back so that it would be nearly comparable in size with what it was many years ago.
It was a matter of grave concern to us because the codfish industry is our national industry. Some of us had been working and had felt that the marketing of our salt codfish had to be taken out of the organization which had been handling it, and that the marketing should be done through the Department of Trade and Commerce and through the highest levels of government. That step was taken a few months ago when, by agreement with our provincial government, authority was passed over to the Department of Trade and Commerce here to look into the marketing conditions of our salt codfish industry and to see what could be done. The measure of the stature of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is this. Within a week he set the wheels of his department in motion. Within three months we have already had three profitable trade agreements and possibly we may soon have a

Supply-Trade and Commerce fourth. Those are facts, Mr. Chairman, that I do not think should go unnoticed in the House of Commons.
We now feel far better about our salt codfish market than we have felt for many years. We now feel that we have begun to market our salt codfish in the right manner. We feel that we are now getting this national industry of ours back on a sound footing. I do not think the opportunity should pass without someone from my province saying a word about what has happened. When I go back home-and I hope to very shortly-I believe a different feeling will exist amongst our fishermen. I believe they will now have a confidence that they have not had for many years that our marketing problems are in the way of being solved. I believe they will feel free to go fishing again. It is my opinion that when they finish up the fishing season this year, they will feel far happier than they have felt for many years. I throw no bouquets in this chamber but I merely say this. .It was the energy, foresight and business experience of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that brought this situation about, and I think the committee should be told that fact.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, at this stage I will confine myself to clearing up several points that have arisen. In his remarks of a moment ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce seemed to be extremely touchy on this subject of the extent to which Canada's trading eggs were being placed in the American basket and about the concern expressed by some of us on this side of the house over that fact and over the fact that the American market, surveyed over the long years, has not been too satisfactory. Conditions have arisen there when the Canadian producer received scant consideration. We have seen that situation in the past two years, when it suited the convenience of the American congress to enact legislation even in breach of the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Let me say to the minister that the concern which we have expressed as to the dangers resulting from Canada's placing all her trading eggs in one basket is not shared alone by those on this side of the house. We hold the view that the minister expressed when he said that we wish to extend our trade in all parts of the world. Of course we wish to do that. But we in this part of the chamber are concerned-and rightly so-that the minister takes such an easy-going, nonchalant attitude about the way in which our export trade to our traditional market in Great Britain drops and the way in which we lose that market, as long as he has in the United States a place

from which to buy or, to a lesser extent, a place to which to sell. When we have an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States of some $800 million, as we had last year, that fact apparently does not give the minister any cause for concern.
Mr. Chairman, I have said that we on this side of the chamber are not the only ones concerned about this matter of the eggs being put in one basket. Will you listen to this, sir? This is a statement reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of September 12, 1952. I will read the statement and then I will give you the author of it. The statement reads as follows:
Canada's economic position, at present strong, also has a weakness, . . .
"That weakness is that Canada depends so much upon the United States . . . Canadians can never be freed from the fear of a slump in the U.S., for which we would not in any way be responsible and which we could do little to control."
Those are the words of the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: So what?

I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce could profit by the comments of his colleague and take a word of warning instead of preserving this easy-going, nonchalant attitude that everything is rosy.
The next thing upon which I should like to comment is the interjection that came from the minister and from his parliamentary assistant during my remarks earlier today concerning what they said was the sale of Canadian wheat to Russia. Mr. Chairman, I could not believe my ears, and I suggested that Canadian sales of wheat to Russia would not amount to anything of any substance. On consulting the official records of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year 1953 I find that our exports to Russia for the year 1953 amounted to $478. If you look up the details, you will find that the record does not show any sales of wheat to Russia.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What about the year 1954?
If there are available some figures for the year 1954, it would be interesting indeed to see them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You read the evening paper to keep up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I appreciate the interest of my hon. friend in the trade commissioner service, and I am glad that he has had an opportunity to visit some of the offices of the service. The more people do that, the more they will appreciate the calibre of the men we have in the service. We do make every effort to bring home to Canadian businessmen the fact that this service is available to them. The department publishes a magazine called Foreign Trade which comes out every two weeks and has a very wide circulation. It contains up to the minute news from our trade commissioners abroad and often articles about special conditions in one of the countries where the service is represented.
We also bring the trade commissioners home to Canada every three years and send them on a tour across the country. That tour of duty lasts about six months, and they are supposed to contact every businessman who has any interest in their particular area, explain the conditions to him, find out the problems in which the Canadian businessman is interested and work out a plan for closer co-operation in the future. That tour is taken before the man gets his holiday leave. After a year in Canada he goes back to his post with fresh business contacts in this country.
As my hon. friend said, I believe we have fifty-one offices at the moment. New offices under consideration are at Hamburg in Germany, Salisbury in Rhodesia, Accra on the Gold Coast, and Istanbul in Turkey, and we are again considering reopening the office in Los Angeles. We try to keep the service up to the requirements of Canadian businessmen. As soon as we find a particular interest in an area that is not well served we correct that by either transferring an office from a less important position or opening a new office in the area with which we are concerned.
Examinations for the candidates for the service are held annually. We take university men and give them special training before sending them into the field. They have a year's training in Canada in a special course arranged by the department and are then sent out in junior positions in the field and are given the opportunity to become fully experienced under an experienced trade commissioner. After we are satisfied with their ability they are promoted to independent posts. I may say that I have been tremendously impressed with this service. I have been impressed with the way our officers work at a problem. After all, there are

no rewards for them. The reward for the businessman is that he will probably make a substantial profit if the transaction is carried out. The only reward for a trade commissioner is the satisfaction of having helped the businessman carry out the transaction.
I have seen these men working days on end on one particular transaction, perhaps a transaction involving a few million dollars. They have had the satisfaction of seeing the transaction completed; they have put in their report, and that is that. They turn to the next transaction. I must say that I think it is a great credit to the service that that kind of enthusiasm can be maintained. I am glad indeed that my hon. friend had the opportunity of meeting commissioners in the field.

recommended to the government that we have a second transmitter in Ottawa that would service this particular part of the country, similar to that which we give in Montreal. At that time the matter was delayed because of the fact that we thought it would require an additional appropriation of money in order to build a transmitter. The situation is that at the present time we have plans and have awarded a contract for the C.B.C. station in Ottawa that is linked by microwave with Buffalo, Montreal and Toronto.

I do not know that I can say anything more at this time. We hope that in a short time, with the completion of our stations in Halifax and Winnipeg, we will have a chain of stations covering Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, and Halifax. Let me give hon. members an example with reference to microwave connections. We can only connect these stations in two ways, either by coaxial cable or by microwave. The microwave in this district was built by the Bell Telephone Company for the purposes of carrying out their policy of having a better method of intercommunication between places for their long distance telephone service. This system has worked out to be very useful for intercommunication between these cities for television purposes, and we pay them a rental for this daily communication system between Buffalo, Montreal, Ottawa, and Toronto of something in the neighbourhood of $250,000 a year.
It is our policy to extend that microwave system from Toronto to Hamilton, Kitchener, London, and Windsor, and in the east from Montreal to Quebec city. We will have to undertake at some time or other an extension of the service east and west from Winnipeg and finally from Vancouver east, and the ultimate objective which we aim to accomplish is that all of our C.B.C. stations from the east coast to the west will be connected up by microwave, and having done that we can then establish a trans-Canada television system.

Now, there are just two or three other matters on which I might add a word, and that is with reference to the criticism we have had of the C.B.C., not only in controlling the C.B.C., if you wish to call it that, but the commercial situation and the alternative proposition submitted as to a separate commission. The question has been raised of the establishment of a separate commission to take over the regulatory powers of the C.B.C., and I wish to point out once again that at the request of the government this question was very carefully and exhaustively studied by the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. The commission recommended strongly against any such proposal and came out in favour of the continuance of the present system.
The government accepted and still accepts the views of the commission which made such a thorough study of all the factors involved. The idea of a separate commission probably seems attractive to a number of people who have not looked carefully into the subject, and it seems to me that this point of view, often accepted without careful consideration, is in many cases helped along by interested propaganda.
I have noted, for instance, that very often statements in favour of a separate commission come from areas where all the newspapers also have private radio interests. I think it is apparent that, at the time, many of those who advocated a separate commission had not thought a great deal about the matter since the statements and arguments which are made are often conflicting. From what I have seen, the recent demands of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters were to set up a commission which would have none of the powers at present held by the C.B.C. Under their proposals these powers would simply vanish. In other words, there would be no one at all in a position to make regulations to limit abuses in the use of the public air channels, or of licences to carry on stations in the country in the interests of maintaining a national system. I think anyone supporting the idea of a separate commission should carefully consider what is involved.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that that pretty well covers the matters which required answers, and I will leave these matters there and deal with any further questions as they are raised. On the next item I have a statement to make with reference to international shortwave, its operation, and policy.

Yes, and I will come back to that later.
I wish to make a comment on the point last dealt with by the minister, namely, the matter of the separate regulatory commission. I shall deal with two aspects of that matter. The minister laid great emphasis upon the report of the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences, commonly known as the Massey report. But I would like to point out to the house that in that respect there was a majority report and a minority report.
It is quite true that the majority report recommended that there be no change in the dual function now exercised by the C.B.C., that is to say. the function of carrying on a nation-wide broadcasting system, and at the same time carrying out a regulatory function over all forms of broadcasting in Canada. But there was a minority report by a very eminent member of that royal commission, Dr. Arthur Surveyer, and I am prepared to say that if hon. members will address themselves with an open mind to the majority report and the minority report I think they will find the recommendations in the minority report overwhelmingly sound and convincing in their logic.
Now, sir, the minister has chosen to introduce another subject in this latter regard which cannot, if it is taken seriously, have any other effect than to confuse the issue. He has brought in the matter of a proposal which he ascribes to the Canadian Association of Broadcasters to the effect that the regulatory functions be dispensed with. That is not the recommendation I put forward when this matter was debated on June 4.
Whatever regulatory functions are required can be confided to the commission. That, in my submission, is the sound way to proceed. It is no part of the proposal for a separate regulatory commission that the commission be denuded of all regulatory power. Surely that would be a contradiction in terms. Let us therefore, Mr. Chairman, approach this question, when there is opportunity, on its merits without its being confused by the kind of issue that the minister has seen fit to introduce.
What is proposed is that there be a separation of these two functions that are now

discharged by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There would be no interference with its operation. It would carry on as an operating body, operating a nation-wide system of broadcasting; but those regulatory functions that it now exercises over the private stations that are, in many respects, its rivals and competitors, would be carried out by a separate regulatory body. The public interest would not be compromised in any way at all. There would be a separate regulatory commission of a public nature appointed by and responsible to public authority. Let us therefore have that question decided on its merits, Mr. Chairman, and not have it confused by insinuations that inherent in that proposal is any suggestion whatever of abandoning the regulatory functions that are now exercised in general.
I make this further comment and this one only. We have a direct parallel in the way in which regulation is exercised in this country over the railways. It is a regulation that applies equally to the publicly-owned Canadian National Railways and the privately-owned Canadian Pacific Railway as well as other privately-owned railways in Canada. We would not think of confiding to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways the regulatory powers over its private competitors that are now exercised by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. What we are recommending in this important field of communication is that there be in that field a separate regulatory board clothed with functions similar to those now exercised in the field of transport by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. The C.B.C. would carry on its operating functions in the same way as the Canadian National Railway Company carries on its operating functions but under the general regulatory powers of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada.
