While the minister is musing a little bit over those answers-although he may have them on the tip of his tongue-I want to make one comment on his further announcement of government policy concerning the independent regulatory body. The minister put great emphasis upon the fact that the royal commission on the arts and sciences had recommended that the policy being pursued should be continued. He went on to put forward the negative angle, namely that they recommended that no other body be set up as a regulatory body. That is all right. We know what the royal commission recommended. But I do not believe that any royal commission is infallible. Even though they may have gone into the study very carefully and have arrived at a conclusion which they themselves, of course, think is a conscientious and proper conclusion, nevertheless royal commissions are not infallible. They may be wrong.
There is another point I wish to make here. The minister said at the same time-and he used the phrase no less than three times- that those who were recommending a separate regulatory body had not looked carefully enough into the subject. He mentioned

Supply-National Revenue that point twice and he concluded by saying that he hoped those who recommended such a regulatory body would consider carefully what is involved. Mention was made of that point three times. I am afraid the minister overemphasized it, at least. He is not fooling anyone here. The people who have recommended the separate regulatory body cannot be said to be men who do not go carefully into a study of the thing they are going to propose. He may be able to say that concerning us who sit here and who are interested in, but not vitally connected with, radio interests. However, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters have men who know their business. They are on a par with-I will not say they are above-any radio officials, radio engineers or men who think in terms of radio policy who sit on the government side of the house or who are connected with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They are men who are just as capable in the radio field as anyone else. You cannot find better anywhere. They have gone into the matter carefully. They know all the angles with respect to a separate regulatory body.
I still hope the time will come when we will see that. I think it will be better. I am not going to say that radio policy will be administered any better but certainly in a free country where we believe in freedom of competition such a thing is desirable. I have a few other questions along an entirely different line, but first I would ask the minister if he would care to answer these questions now.

The answer to the question of the hon. member for Macleod with reference to the situation in Ottawa is that there will be two channels. There will be one station, one building and one of the channels, which will involve the purchase and installation of a new transmitter, will give entirely French programs and the other channel will give entirely English programs. We have a precedent for that in what we did in the city of Montreal. His other question, as I remember it, was with reference to the linking up of the system. That will probably take two or three years.

I think we will be doing very well if we get it in two or three years. The minister is very encouraging in that respect. My other questions are of a little different nature. I want to be fair, and if these matters do not come under the minister's department but rather under the Department of Transport I will be happy if he will inform me and I will leave them until the transport estimates are before us. I understand that government radio policy does not permit the building of transmitters with what is known 

as composite equipment. In other words, government radio policy today is that if a station wants to build a transmitter a licence will not be granted unless the equipment is manufactured by one of the standard equipment companies. If that is so, I should like to know why, because according to my information I understand that certain stations in the United States have been able to cut their costs almost in half by reason of their engineers being able to assemble parts from here and there, sometimes manufacture them themselves, and build a transmitter for around $80,000 instead of approximately $150,000 which it would have otherwise cost.
I wonder whether the minister would care to answer that question for me, and a similar question along almost the same line of thought. I also understand that radio policy does not permit radio stations to transmit by what is known as a sort of pick-up antenna but that they must of necessity have lines for which of course a very expensive fee is charged. I understand this is permitted in the United States, which cuts the cost considerably. I am told that an ordinary station can save in the neighbourhood of $40,000 a year. That figure may not apply in Canada, but in the United States about $40,000 can be saved by being able to broadcast by means of a pick-up system rather than by using lines.
Evidently these matters come within the minister's department, and I have a third question which I am sure does. It has to do with the customs duty charged on motion picture films for television. I understand the same customs duty charges are imposed on the importation of films for use on television as are imposed on films that are used in motion picture theatres. The reason I ask this question is that there is quite a difference between the two. In other words, a theatrical distributing agency imports films, pays the duty on them, and then they can be used in several hundred theatres throughout Canada. I understand that the duty on an ordinary moving picture film amounts to about $60.
If such films are to be shown on television and an independent station has to pay a duty of that amount to import a film that is to be used just once, and if they have to have different films for many different programs, then the charge becomes rather terrific. Of course it has to be carried into the cost of operating the station. The sponsors would have to pay, which would mean that the cost to the sponsor would be tremendously high. I wonder whether the minister would care to answer these three questions for me.

The answer to the first two questions is that they are matters involving technical requirements, and that of course is decided by the Department of Transport. With reference to the matter of the customs duty on films for television and films for the motion picture industry, I do not know that consideration has been given to the question of use. They are both films. They are classified under the customs tariff as films and the duty is the same in both cases as far as I know. The matter of the usage has not been given any consideration to date under the customs tariff.

That is my point. Because there is no difference the television station has to pay a duty of approximately $60 for one film while the theatre interests can get the same films for $60 and use it thousands of times if they want to. There is one motion picture film in Ottawa today that is entering its third month of showing. If $60 had to be paid every time the film was shown, the cost would be terrific. Since that is so, would the minister not give some consideration to a reduction of duty on films for television purposes?
I will bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance, who usually has to do with customs tariff rates.
When a film is returned to the country of origin is the duty not refunded?
Part of it. There is a partial refund depending on the length of time that it has been in this country.

I should like to ask the minister a very short question. Last Friday night he said that there must be sufficient national coverage before there could be more than two stations in certain areas. With reference to his statement tonight about the microwave system, does the minister's statement mean that the microwave system will have to be complete before there is alternate service?
The answer is, not necessarily.

I should like to ask a question with regard to television in Edmonton. I understand that a licence has been granted to some private enterprise there for the construction of transmitters to transmit television programs. My first question is, does the minister know when we may expect to get television programs in Edmonton? My second question is, within what radius from the transmitters will people in an area be expected to obtain these programs?
Supply-National Revenue

The matter is entirely up to the people who have the licence for the private station. They have to order the transmitter, and it depends entirely upon when the transmitter is delivered to them, and when they construct their building, as to when they can commence operations. This is a matter with which the C.B.C. has nothing to do. In the ordinary course of events it takes anywhere from six months to a year; some stations have come along quicker.
The area of transmission of television equipment is usually a radius of about sixty miles from the centre, and that again depends a good deal on the terrain. I might point this out for the benefit of hon. members, that when you broadcast radio waves they will jump an obstruction, for instance, a mountain that is not too high, and that wave is still continued to the point of reception. It is entirely different with television. You must have a direct line from the point of transmission to the point of reception in order to get good reception. It is for that reason that television waves are received much better over water than in hilly terrain. We believe that the technological development in the science of television transmission may overcome some of those difficulties in the years ahead.

May I ask a supplementary question? When this licence was granted to this private enterprise, was it not conditional that the transmitters would be completed within a certain period of time? In other words, could they carry on with this construction for the next five years?

No, that is a matter between the company that obtains a licence and the Department of Transport. In this particular case, or any other case, I do not know whether or not the Department of Transport has stipulated a time within which that television station shall be in operation.

I should like to speak for just a moment or two about the C.B.C. and the television stations that we are building across the country. I should like to commend the minister upon the splendid programs we have received over the radio from the C.B.C. The majority of them are of first-class quality.
Just so that we would not ever have a repetition of a program that was broadcast on March 10 in the form of an appreciation of Eugene O'Neill, I should like to tell the house some of the things that were broadcast on that program. This was the filthiest program I have ever heard over any radio. The cursing that went on in it was absolutely disgusting. There were some 125 pages of script, and I believe in 22 places they took

Supply-National Revenue the Lord's name in vain. It was a very low type of program. Eugene O'Neill may have been a very great writer, but I do not believe it was fitting or becoming for our radio broadcasting system to pay tribute to the man in a manner that would be disgusting to most Christian homes in the dominion.
If the chairman will allow me, I should like to quote one of the phrases that came over the radio in the course of that program. A Mr. Burke, one of the characters in the play, was speaking to a girl by the name of Anna, and he said something like this:
God's curse on you, you slut; you would be sleeping with any man for a dollar or two.
I do not think that is the proper type of program to be broadcast on a system that gives the high-class service to radio that the C.B.C. programs do generally. Certainly the minister should call the attention of the censors to the fact they let that type of program get through.
I hesitate, because of one program that was absolutely vile, to castigate the service as a whole; it has been excellent. If I want to turn on my radio, hunting a good program at random I try a program from the C.B.C. because the likelihood of my finding an intelligent and interesting program is greater there than anywhere else, except for our local station which is exceptional. I do ask the minister if he would call to the attention of the officials that there are people in the dominion who object to that type of program. I feel that if a little common sense were used the man who would pick that type of program would not be allowed to pick many more programs for the C.B.C.
Having said that, I wish to say this is my only criticism of the C.B.C. I commend the minister most highly for his determination and courage, at this difficult time when expenditures are high, in achieving a series of broadcasting television stations in this dominion from east to west. It would have been very easy at this time for a man with less determination to have allowed our country to have television broadcasts from north to south. In other words, we would be flooded with programs brought in from the United States. The western states would influence our stations in western Canada, and the eastern provinces would be influenced by programs from the eastern states. That would have been a simple thing to do. It would have been a sort of natural evolution to allow that to happen.
He did not do that. He insisted that we have a trans-Canada system. If there was ever a time when we needed to keep our dominion united, it is now. This is one of


the things that will do that very well. I commend him for the resistance he has put up to anyone and everyone-it comes not only from the official opposition but from members of his own party as well-to allowing our stations to be broken up so that we would have a north-south television system on the continent rather than an east-west television system for Canada.
If I were picking any particular program on which the minister should be commended, I would say to him that the broadcast of the Grey cup would likely be followed by more people across Canada than any other program. It was certainly very well done. I was not fortunate enough to be present at the game this year, but I honestly believe I saw it better over television than I would have if I had been sitting in a seat in the stands. It was certainly well done.

On behalf of the electors of my constituency, both English-speaking and French-speaking, it is a great pleasure for me to thank the Minister of National Revenue for his quick and gentlemanly decision to allow a French station in this area. As I said in my last speech on this subject, this is an illustration of the ability of this government to give good administration from one corner of the country to the other. I thank the minister again, and I wish that my electors would write and thank him and the cabinet for doing so splendidly.

May I be permitted, Mr. Chairman, in the name of my electors to thank the minister for the good news we have received this evening. I was not in the house, but was told by somebody else that our request for a second station has been granted. When I started to speak the other day, I said that I knew the minister and the government were sympathetic and would listen to my request. So, in the name of my electors, both French and English, I thank you, from the bottom of my heart.

May I answer the hon. member for Wellington South with respect to the Eugene O'Neill broadcast, if we may call it that. I am sorry if it hurt the sensibilities of some of his electors, in the constituency in which he lives. But there is always another side to it. We received many more letters of commendation for that broadcast than we received protests against it.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to revert to a question which has been discussed many times in the house, and which will continue to be discussed as long as the situation is not remedied. I go back to the question

of the dual capacity of the C.B.C.-the triple capacity, I might say-as judge, litigant and policeman.
I have never been able to understand how anyone can argue seriously that this situation is substantially different from that in the railways, where no one would even dream of suggesting that the Canadian National Railways should perform a dual or triple function.
Tonight I notice that the minister, trying to justify a distinction which I never heard anyone successfully justify, referred to the Massey report. Well, I said to myself, per

iaps the answer is in this report. Perhaps I have been wrong all along. Perhaps we will find the answer.
I have read what the Massey report says, and I do not find that it contains anything that even approaches a reason for continuing the situation. The majority report says this, at page 288, under the heading "Procedure of the Board of Governors and a Right of Appeal":
In the interests of the national system and of the country as a whole, we recommend rejection of the demands by private broadcasters for a separate regulatory body and for the privilege of forming private networks.
I propose to read further; but I think I am correct in saying that that is the only sentence approaching an argument. I shall read more from this paragraph, and if anyone can discern an argument from what I shall read later, then let him do so. I shall repeat the first sentence-
In the interests of the national system and of the country as a whole, we recommend-
I do not know whether the minister regards that as an argument. To my mind there is not even a featherweight of an argument in it. It is only expressing the view that they have. There is no attempt made to make a distinction from the railway situation, which I suggest it resembles in the closest manner.
But that is the recommendation after all these representations have been made.
I accept the minister's suggestion, if he can find in this book any reasons-
The argument is not given there-only the conclusions.
Has the hon. member read the broadcasting act?
Does the Secretary of State wish to make a speech?

I was asking a question.
Supply-National Revenue

I wish to continue by reading further from this section. The Massey commission does recommend some alleviation of the position of private broadcasters, because it recommends that they should have the right to be heard, instead of its being purely a matter of privilege. I shall read what they say:
At present, when the board of governors contemplates the recommendation of the suspension of a licence or a change in the regulations, the private stations receive notice of the matter and are given the opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel, and at a public session if they so desire. These concessions are granted as privileges. Considerations of justice suggest that they be recognized fully as rights.
Then they continue to discuss the question of the right of appeal. I need not read that part.
What I am still waiting for is someone to give a reason why it would be unfair to do what I submit would be the natural instinct of any reasonable man if a situation of this kind were presented to him. What has been done in connection with the railways would be regarded as the obviously right thing to do. I am still waiting for anyone to give a substantial reason differentiating the two cases.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two things to say. I do not propose to repeat the arguments advanced last Friday by the hon. member for Eglinton in connection with the monopoly enjoyed by the C.B.C., but I do propose asking the minister one or two questions with regard to the situation out west.
I appreciate the difficulty there is in conducting discussion of the estimates in this fashion, when we dealt with them in a limited degree last Friday and then they are suddenly placed before us this evening after the dinner recess. I noticed however in the minister's remarks on June 4-and I was here and heard them-that he dealt with the policy of the C.B.C. in connection with tele vision, and said, in effect, that in certain areas television stations would be set up under the C.B.C., and that in other areas where the population was in excess of 25,000 private stations might be able to enter the field: Perhaps I should quote what the minister said, so as to avoid any misunderstanding. These are his words as reported at page 5557 of Hansard:
It may not be long before there is a sufficient degree of national coverage to justify the government and the C.B.C. giving consideration to permitting two and perhaps in some cases more than two stations in certain areas. It is anticipated that, in due course, private stations will be permitted in

Supply-National Revenue areas covered by C.B.C. stations, and the C.B.C. may establish stations in some areas originally covered by private stations.
The point I wish to make is this, that in Winnipeg the C.B.C. television station has just recently opened. I believe the opening date was May 31. I read in the press that it has survived the violent storm which shattered different parts of that city. It must not be overlooked however that the provision of television in Winnipeg has been delayed for a long time. It has been available to the people in the central provinces for two or three years, but only now has it become available in Winnipeg and Manitoba.
Now that we have an announcement from the minister to the effect that his program is being modified to a certain degree, and that a second outlet is to be provided in Ottawa, for good and sufficient reasons-to which I have no objection-I suggest to him that he might go further and modify the policy he has laid down. Certainly it should be clarified before the end of this evening. I will suggest one modification. He has said that in due course private stations will be permitted in some areas, and that in due course the C.B.C. may invade areas occupied by private stations.
Surely the policy-making of the department has gone far enough to determine whether it would be a year, two years or three years. Some announcement should be made as to when additional stations may be allowed in certain areas, so that those who propose entering the television field may make proper plans. I ask the minister this question. At what stage will a decision be reached to permit private stations to enter a field that at the moment is pre-empted by a government station? My suggestion is that the policy as announced by the minister last week and the policy that he pronounced a year ago be modified to this extent, that in those areas of Canada where there has been so much delay in providing television under government auspices there should not be the same delay in permitting private stations to enter the field now being served by the government television station.
What is going to happen is this. In the course of time, how many years I do not know, the minister will determine that, in the areas in the central provinces now served by government-owned television stations, private stations may enter the field, and then with a delay of two or three years, out in Winnipeg and elsewhere in other parts of Canada similar action may be taken. I suggest to him that he reverse this trend of events, and that, in view of the delay which

has already been caused in giving government television sponsored programs out west, at an earlier stage he permit private stations to enter that particular field if they so desire. I for one cannot see why it might not be done almost immediately.
What is going to happen to determine that at some particular point, one year from now, six months from now, or five years from now, the government will decide that it is time for private television stations to enter the field already pre-empted by a government television station? Can the minister not modify this policy at this point, and in view of this delay that I have mentioned permit a private station, if it so desires, to set up operation, say in the city of Winnipeg? Let the minister bear this in mind as well. In the central provinces that lie so close to the United States border and to the large population areas of that country, there are ever so many more TV outlets available for those who have TV sets on this side of the line, which can tune in to ever so many stations. In the city of Winnipeg and elsewhere in other parts of Canada those extra TV sources will not be available, and consequently I would think that would be a consideration to permit private stations to operate in areas of that nature, so that the people of those areas would have more than one television station to which they might direct their aerial.
Naturally, in certain areas of Canada we will always face this problem. No longer in radio is it a problem, and it should not for any great length of time be a problem in television, but at the moment it is, and in certain areas of Canada for a number of years there will be certain restrictions on the number of programs that can be received. I suggest this is a method by which those areas may be more adequately served and may be brought into a comparable position with the more fortunate people located in the central provinces closer to the United States television stations.
I put these matters before the minister for his consideration and suggest that, in view of his policy announced tonight, he may now consider a further modification in favour of those areas which are less likely to be served adequately with television at the present time.

Before the minister replies to the various questions that were put to him with respect to television, I wish to raise one point in connection with our local area. When he replies to the numerous questions and complaints about the fact that they have not two television stations, I wish he would

tell me what is the situation with respect to Halifax. We have had various statements in the press from time to time with respect to the station there to the effect that they are going to buy the land, they have bought the land, and that they are about to erect these stations. Quite recently I saw that one of the engineers made a statement that sometime in December the television station would be in operation. That is very encouraging, but when the minister replies tonight to the various questions that have been asked that are of interest to other parts of Canada, I wish he would reply to us. Our complaint is not that we have not a dual outlet at the moment. We have not any in the maritimes. The position is such that at least in the eastern part of our country we cannot get television from the United States stations and we are dependent upon the C.B.C. to inaugurate their service. When the minister replies I hope that he will be able to confirm the newspaper story which appeared the other day and which, as I said, was made by one of his responsible officials, and which has not been confirmed by him, that we could expect the station to be in operation in December. If the minister considers that the change in policy in other places applies to Halifax, perhaps we shall have competition at least so that we can have two stations there.

Before the minister replies there are one or two comments that I should like to make at this time with respect to the C.B.C. I want to commend the C.B.C. and a great many of those programs which I as a teacher have been particularly interested in. As a teacher of literature I find that such programs as the productions of "Julius Caesar", "Macbeth" and "Hamlet" have been of great benefit to all teachers throughout Canada who have had the opportunity of listening to those broadcasts and having their students listen to them. The C.B.C. should be commended on the excellence of those productions.
We have had some criticism of the work of the C.B.C. Some of that criticism I find it very difficult to understand. When we were discussing the estimates the last day the C.B.C. was under discussion we had some criticism of the fact that the C.B.C. was trying to impose culture on the people of Canada. On the other hand, we had people criticizing the C.B.C. for producing programs that were not cultural. We had the Leader of the Opposition, I believe, referring to some of the wrestling programs broadcast on Saturday evenings from Chicago. Well, I suggest you cannot have it both ways. You
Supply-National Revenue cannot criticize the C.B.C. in one breath because it is trying to impose culture on the people of Canada, and then in the next breath criticize their broadcasting of wrestling matches on television on Saturday nights. I expect the reasons the C.B.C. carries the wrestling matches on Saturday night is that a great many Canadians enjoy watching wrestling matches over television. We should be fair in our estimate of the C.B.C. If we are going to listen to criticism of that organization on the score that it is trying to impose culture, and then at the next moment criticize it because it yields to public demand, I think great inconsistency is revealed there.
There is one matter that should be noted. I recall reading in the press a number of days ago an address given before the United Church conference meeting in Ontario in which one of the speakers pointed out that in the United States-and I am speaking from memory now-eleven corporations in that country controlled 80 per cent of the television broadcast programs. That fact in itself brings home to the people of Canada the necessity of providing television programs that will meet the needs of the Canadian people.
I realize that if we are going to leave radio and television to those who look upon that particular field as a means of commercial exploitation, of presenting programs, together with the advertising commercials that will yield revenue to those companies, we are taking a very shortsighted view of radio and television.
There is one particular aspect of this problem I would like to draw to the attention of the minister and that is, if my understanding is correct, that in my own province television licences have been granted. I believe there have been two applicants, one in my own constituency of Regina City and another one in the city of Saskatoon. I have received some correspondence from constituents who have expressed some alarm over the fact that the C.B.C. is ignoring the province of Saskatchewan, and that they are leaving television broadcasts entirely to private outlets.
I am not for one moment complaining of the granting of licences to private television stations in Regina or in the city of Saskatoon, but I am suggesting that, in keeping with the policy which now prevails in so far as C.B.C. radio broadcasting is concerned, the C.B.C. ought to revise its plans and see whether or not my province can be included in the television plans of the C.B.C. I think some arrangement could be reached whereby, for example, the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw

Supply*-National Revenue could be reached or whereby the three major cities of Saskatchewan could be served by television under the auspices of the C.B.C.
At the present time we have the C.B.C. transmitter CBK at Watrous which serves a great need in the province of Saskatchewan, but there are a number of people in Saskatchewan who are concerned over the fact that the C.B.C. at the present time is apparently prepared to leave television broadcasting to private outlets in that province.
I should therefore like to ask the minister at this time to seriously consider the provision of television broadcasting by the C.B.C. in the province of Saskatchewan. I am not pretending to be an authority on television broadcasting, and I am not suggesting that some scheme might be worked out at the present time. But I am suggesting that the television authorities in the C.B.C. might find it possible to establish a C.B.C. station in the province of Saskatchewan at some central point which will serve the main population areas of that province in order that we might obtain in the field of TV the excellent service which I feel the people of the province have obtained in the field of radio from our prairie transmitter CBK.

Mr. Chairman, I want to answer briefly some of the questions which have been asked. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings raised the question of the development of the television station at Halifax. Let me say to him that the property has been acquired, the equipment has all been ordered, and it now depends very much upon the delivery of that equipment as to when we will complete the station in Halifax. We expect that if we get the delivery of the equipment we will be in operation in Halifax before the end of the year.
With reference to the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre,
I am not going to go into detail with reference to the answering of his question on policy because I feel I am being baited and tantalized in an effort to have me announce something new with reference to the policy of the C.B.C. There is nothing new to announce. We shall continue to carry out the policy which was laid down a year or so ago. When that policy is changed, and it becomes government and C.B.C. policy, announcements will be made to the house if it is in session, or to the public.
Mr. Chairman-

Pardon me. May I answer the question asked by the hon. member for Regina City? We appear to have a rather anomalous situation here. This vote covers a loan of $3 million and what we are asking


for is money to complete the program which was announced a year ago and which we told the house then would cost a certain amount of money. The hon. member for Regina City now comes along and wants more money for expenditure in Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan has one of the best sound radio systems in the world with a high powered station at Watrous.
But how about TV?

We will come to that. On my own observation I would say they have better radio reception in Saskatchewan than in almost any other part of Canada. In Regina and Saskatoon licences have been granted for two private television stations which will pick up the service of the C.B.C. and obtain sustaining programs from them either by films or by kinescopic transmission. If the time comes when the C.B.C. fails in any respect to complete its link or give a better service to the people of Saskatchewan the matter will then be given further consideration.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has suggested that he was being baited and tantalized with reference to C.B.C. policy, but there was no such intention on my part. Indeed, the minister is being tantalizing in declining to answer the question I asked with regard to a clarification of the policy which was expressed in very general terms, and I do not see why he could not elucidate without doing harm to anyone. He has already declared this policy in the past and I quoted his words. I quote them again:
-it may not be long before there is a sufficient degree of national coverage to justify the government and the C.B.C. giving consideration to permitting two and perhaps in some cases more than two stations in certain areas.
Well, at this stage, two years after the minister has declared his policy, could he not tell us what is meant by "a sufficient degree of national coverage"? That is what I was after, so that those people who want to enter the private television field may be able to make some plans.
Does "a sufficient degree of national coverage" mean the setting up of a government television station in each province? I think that is what the minister said somewhat later on. And in addition, how long does it have to be in operation before coverage is considered complete? The minister, having to his satisfaction dealt with part of my statement, did not make any comment with regard to my suggestion that he permit at an early date the establishment of a private TV station in the city of Winnipeg, and elsewhere in those parts of Canada

where there are limited facilities at the moment because other TV stations are not in close proximity to these cities and areas in Canada, urely there is nothing wrong in making a suggestion of that nature, and I think the minister might have dealt with it.

While the minister is considering that point I would like to ask a question which follows in part what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had to say. The city of Winnipeg will have a TV station which I understand will have an effective radius of about 80 miles. That, of course, leaves out a very important sector of Manitoba, and perhaps I might even say the most important sector.
I wonder if the C.B.C. has any plans for the balance of the province of Manitoba. For example, the cities of Brandon, Portage la Prairie, Neepawa, Dauphin, and others who are vitally interested in this, would like to know if any plans are now being made in that regard. I believe the minister will agree that that will have a very direct bearing on the volume of, shall we say, agitation for private licences. If the people in the rest of the province of Manitoba feel that there is a C.B.C. service coming in, they are not so likely to join in the hue and cry for smaller television stations under private licence. It is not that we have any objection to private television stations but we believe that it would be better to have a network which would serve at least the greater proportion of the province of Manitoba. I hope the minister will have something to say about the rest of the province outside of the greater Winnipeg area.

I come from a town or
constituency that is just on the frontier. The people up around my part of the country are quite used to snow. But any day in the summer when the two television sets are turned on, we are reminded of the country and the abundance of snow we have. That is all we can see on those two television sets. I think this would be an opportune time for the minister to state now whether the government is working on a plan to extend the scope and the distance-*
Is that the snow belt?

That is just about the sort of remark one would expect from the hon. member. Let him either get in or get out. I have the floor. Let the hon. member behave himself. He could not convince my people of anything.
Supply-National Revenue
I should like to know what the situation is because private corporations are, as I understand it, at the present time endeavouring to obtain permits to establish television stations in that district. However, it might not be an advisable thing to establish those local television distributing stations if the government were extending the distance they had to cover in a short period of time. That is a matter that right now is of vital interest to the people where I reside. Can the minister give us some information with regard to the matter?

I think the information the hon. gentleman wants is that any of those communities or localities are quite free to make application to establish a private television station and that there is not in the near or foreseeable future the likelihood of these outer communities, as we might call them, having C.B.C. service unless technological improvements in the broadcasting of television are of such an extent that the area which we now have is extended, or the radius which will be covered by a high-powered station.

Then what that means is this, Mr. Chairman. We taxpayers are paying for the over-all government provision of television and we are now being called upon to get something local; they will probably not be nearly as fine broadcasts as the bigger centres are getting. Apparently, from what the minister has said, there does not seem to be any hope of the taxpayers who are on the outer fringe receiving any benefits for the taxes they are contributing towards the C.B.C. for its television. Is that right? We receive no benefits. We must establish our own local, small, inexpensive facilities in keeping with our pocketbooks and the results will be according to the expenditure made. That would mean that as far as television broadcasts are concerned, the service enjoyed by the larger centres would be far superior to that enjoyed by the communities on the outer fringe. Is that right?

The hon. gentleman has a misconception as to who pays for television. It is the recipient of television programs who has bought a receiving set and has paid the excise and sales tax on it. Those funds are earmarked. They go to the C.B.C. The individual who lives in a community like that of my hon. friend and who has not a television set and has not purchased one, does not pay anything towards the upkeep of the C.B.C. at all. Our finances are entirely obtained by the matter of allocating to the C.B.C. the excise tax and the sales tax on

Supply-National Revenue radio receiving sets and television sets and tubes; and loans in addition. I may say that they are loans which we expect some day to repay. That is what this one is. Let me say to my hon. friend that if private stations are established by private interests in the communities to which he refers they get, the same as any other station, a service free of charge from the C.B.C.

I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his announcement this evening that Ottawa is to have another C.B.C. station in French. I think I speak on behalf of all the population of this area, English-speaking as well as French-speaking. As I said the other evening, this action will do much to convince the people of the good intentions of the C.B.C. and of the fact that the principles by which it is governed are truly to serve all the population, wherever they may be. We in this area also are satisfied that in due time there will be some private stations which I think would serve us well. We hope that the new French programs will be received by our population in the near future.

I thank the hon. member for Ottawa East for what he has said. I just want to correct what appears to be a misconception in the statement. This is not a second station. Ottawa will have one station with two transmitters and two channels. If it goes out throughout the country that we are building another big building here, it will give a wrong impression. That is not so. Arrangements will be made that two transmitters will be within one building and another channel will be allocated to Ottawa so that you will get French programs over one channel and English programs over the other one. The position will be exactly the same as that which obtains in Montreal.

I thank the minister for raising this matter. That is exactly what I pleaded for the other evening. On those grounds I thought it was possible to have another outlet in Ottawa, because, as the minister has so well said, it would not involve the construction of a station but merely the use of another channel on a new transmitter.

I should like to make a few comments following the suggestions made by the hon. member for Regina City. Those of us who live in Saskatchewan appreciate the splendid service we receive from C.B.C. Watrous. The other day I said that we have not any radio stations in the constituency in which I live. Prior to the establishment of the Watrous station we were at the

mercy of some of the powerful American stations and occasionally we were able to get some of the local stations. Having had the good fortune to have the service over the C.B.C. from Watrous for so many years, we should like the C.B.C. to come into the television field in Saskatchewan instead of turning the field over to private television stations. On Friday I referred to those wise words uttered by the late Lord Bennett when the first radio bill was before parliament; at that time he suggested that this was too valuable a resource for the people to give away for a song. I think that advice given in 1932 is good in 1954. I have always been happy that I have lived in Canada, but never happier than when I visit the United States and have to compare their radio with Canadian radio and their television with Canadian television, where you have to take so much obnoxious advertising with their musical or other programs. I hope the minister will, as soon as possible, come into Saskatchewan in the television field and see to it that the people on the frontiers have the advantages that are now taken for granted in the cities. While it is true that a new station is not being built in Ottawa, the minister has announced that an expenditure of $500,000 is going to be made to bring in the two languages. I am not complaining about that expenditure. But if the people in this area can have the choice of either French or English programs, I think the people on the frontiers should have the privilege of having the much improved television service that the C.B.C. will give.

What progress has been made by the C.B.C. in developing colour television? It is a well known fact that the people of this country who have bought television sets have paid extremely high prices for them. I think it is fair to say that we in Canada have paid almost twice as much for television sets as the same machines would cost in the United States. The television industry in Canada has pretty well saturated the market with black and white television. What is going to be the position of the Canadian people when colour television arrives? I understand it is just about due to be introduced in the United States now. What is going to be the situation in Canada in the case of people who have already purchased television sets? The market has been saturated with black and white television sets, and if colour is to be introduced and people are going to be required to buy new sets, that is coming pretty close to the point of exploitation.
I think some consideration should be given to having sets that will be convertible from

black and white to colour so that if it is desired to change a black and white machine to colour it can be done for a nominal fee instead of having to buy a completely new set. Has the minister given any consideration to that?

I have followed closely the development of colour television, and I may say to the hon. member that we have not spent any money on behalf of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with respect to the development of colour television in Canada. The large companies in the United States have invited us to follow the progress that is being made there. At the present time colour television sets cost from $1,200 to $2,000. I would suggest to the hon. member that if he has in mind some sort of gadget that will change black and white into colour he has got a fortune right before him. They have been working on that for years and have spent millions of dollars but it has not been developed. We in Canada will continue to follow closely the developments with respect to colour television and when it becomes practical we will attempt to introduce it in Canada.
Would the minister make a statement with respect to the question I asked having to do with C.B.C. television plans for the rest of Manitoba outside of the Winnipeg area?

Outside of the city of Winnipeg any individual or company is free to make an application for the establishment of a private television station. Once it is established we will provide it with programs as we do other stations. As I said before, the development of the microwave may bring about sooner than we anticipated the linking up of the main station with private stations in other parts of the province.

What I had in mind was whether the C.B.C. had any intention of installing relay or booster stations at other points in the province in order to provide its own service to a wider area. Is that contemplated?
There is no such thing as a booster station in television.

There are a couple of questions I should like to ask the minister but before doing so I should like to revert for a moment to his remarks regarding the control of broadcasting in the country by a separate regulatory body. I know the minister wants to be fair, but if I understood him aright I must say that either he was not understood as he intended to be or else he was something less than objective as far as the question is 83276-368
Supply-National Revenue concerned. He left the impression with me that the idea of having our publicly owned broadcasting system and our privately owned broadcasting stations both controlled by a separate controlling body was an ill-considered theory advanced by persons who were not very well versed in the field. He left the impression with me that it was considered that it was something approaching a harebrained idea.
I should like to point out that Australia, which has a federal system of government very similar to ours, had a system of radio broadcasting very similar to ours for a number of years, a privately owned system of stations operating opposite a publicly owned system with the publicly owned system controlling broadcasting exactly as in Canada. A few years ago, as the result of a very detailed investigation of the situation, the government of Australia decided to divorce control from operation so far as the publicly owned system was concerned and set up what is known as the Australian broadcasting control board. That was brought into being by the Australian broadcasting control board act which was passed by the previous government to the one now in power in Australia. When that government was defeated at the polls and the opposition came into power they retained the system. I think it must be admitted that there is a very large segment of public opinion in some parts of the world at least which considers that the idea of controlling publicly owned and privately owned broadcasting by a separate board has considerable merit.
I do not want to labour that point, and I pass on to the three small items I want to bring to the minister's attention. The first one has to do with television. I think it can be taken for granted-at least, I hope it can -that if at some future date the C.B.C. decides to broadcast television in colour it will use a system which is compatible with receivers now in use, thus permitting the reception of colour programs in black and white. I have a couple of other points which I suppose are related to the question of control of broadcasting. One has to do with the advertising which is broadcast on both publicly and privately owned stations. It is quite obvious that in the case of other types of publishing, newspapers and so on, people are not forced to pay any attention to the advertising. If we do not like the advertising in the newspaper we skip it, but in the case of broadcasting the thing is in sequence so we have no choice but to listen to or watch the advertising that is thrown at us.

I should like to suggest that it might be advantageous to control the type of advertising more closely. I do not object to advertising as such or the time devoted to it. I think that is a necessary thing in a country such as ours in order to finance our broadcasting at all, but it is the content to which I object. I object to broadcasting advertising which is dramatized and which includes the squalling of sick babies and the moaning of otherwise healthy people who are suddenly stricken ill by lumbago or something of that sort. I think that considerable of that type of advertising is perhaps unnecessary.
I was pleased to hear the minister say again that private television stations that are set up will have sustaining program service supplied to them by the C.B.C. I think that is an excellent thing, and I think it is only fair because the people who watch these network broadcasts pay the excise tax on their receivers the same as the people who have the privilege of watching C.B.C. broadcasts. The raising of funds by way of excise tax is a different system. I feel that the same principle should be applied to sound broadcasting, to some extent at least.
I say that for this reason. Private stations are not permitted to have networks: It is, therefore, in very rare instances that it is economically feasible to put on live programs. These stations have to resort to canned music or canned programs of some sort, and most of those canned programs come from the United States. I should like to see the C.B.C. engaged in the recording of programs for sound transmission in Canada to be used by private stations as much as possible.

May I ask the minister a question based on an earlier statement he made that private television stations would be supplied with certain material from the C.B.C. Can the minister tell me what arrangement is being made between the C.B.C. and private television broadcasting stations with respect to this material? In other words, is there a definite percentage of the broadcasting time which private stations must make available for network programs, or what guarantee have we that the more important C.B.C. network programs will be carried by private stations?

May I answer the last question first, Mr. Chairman? Private stations are obliged to take a minimum amount of material, and presently we are offering more than they can take.
The hon. member for Queens, and other members, have raised again the question of a regulatory body. I am not going to go into
[Mr. MacLean.l

a detailed explanation or reiteration of that argument. This matter has been brought up at successive meetings of the radio committee for a number of years. Detailed arguments were presented to the Massey commission on the subject, and what I am going by, as well as the C.B.C., is the majority report of the commission with reference to the regulatory body, which is the C.B.C. and which has been found to be satisfactory.

From listening to the debate tonight, there is one thing that seems obvious and that is that members are seeking for an alternative to the C.B.C. or vice versa in the television field. Some of the members who have spoken here tonight want the C.B.C. to move in where private television stations are coming into being. On the other hand, we have people who want private television stations to be established where we have C.B.C. service. It would seem to me, therefore, that we, as a people, are looking for an alternative so that we are not confirmed to either one or the other. I think, essentially and basically, that is freedom. I think it is the seeking of freedom that causes the people across the land to want this alternative.
I was interested in what one hon. member had to say about the tax. I think it is interesting to know that the tax on television sets will provide the C.B.C. with funds, although the purchaser may be a viewer of a private station. I feel that is a factor which will benefit the programs the C.B.C. may supply to the private station in carrying out their service. I was interested, also, in what the hon. member for Wellington South had to say about a certain program. I am wondering whether the minister can provide the house with any figures in connection with that program, in view of the answer he gave. I should like also to know if there has been any poll taken of listeners who are able to receive both the C.B.C. and private stations in the same area, to determine the listening audience of the C.B.C. as compared with the private stations. I think that would be very interesting, if the minister has those figures, and I should be glad to hear from him.
Those figures are not available, but we can get answers to those questions and put them on Hansard or give them to the hon. member privately.

I have several questions for the minister. In his statement to the house on June 4, he referred to the four private stations that are now in operation and the sixteen more that have been authorized. May I ask him if he would put on the record tonight the call letters and locations of each

of those stations? I do not suggest he take the time to read that in full now, but he could put it on the record tonight.
The next question I have is as to the budget of the C.B.C. for this forthcoming year. At page 5556 of Hansard of June 4, the minister put on the record the essential items in the operating statement of C.B.C. for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954. Can he give us the figures in the budget for the fiscal year which commenced April 1, 1954, the contemplated revenue and expenditures?
To what did the hon. member refer that was not given on June 4?

The figures given by the minister on the page to which I have referred are the figures for the operations for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954. What I am asking is, what are the figures for the budget for the new fiscal year which commenced April 1,	1954, the contemplated
revenue and contemplated expenditures?

I am informed, Mr. Chairman, we have not the detailed figures on that. The revenue is pretty much as estimated in the estimates. For instance, the vote will be $6,250,000 to provide the requirements of sound broadcasting, and the other for the amount equal to taxes is $15 million. Our expenditures we contemplate, without giving details, will be about equal to the amount of money that is given here by statute.

That is not a very satisfactory explanation. We are asked to provide a loan of $3 million in addition to the other revenue that has been made available to the C.B.C. There is $6,250,000 under the five-year system of handling grants, and then there is the revenue from excise taxes, which last year yielded considerably more than $15 million. Actually last year it yielded about $17 million from both TV and sound sets. The revenue this year has been calculated on the careful side at $15 million. But, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that we are dealing with a very substantial amount of money. Last year the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did not need all the money it received by way of revenue. On the sound operations it finished up with a surplus of $1,091,000, after writing off $515,000 on account of depreciation and obsolescence. On the television side of its operations it finished up with a surplus of $5,331,000 after writing off $425,000 on account of depreciation and obsolescence.
This means that last year, in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, after writing off almost $1 million on account of depreciation and 83276-368J
Supply-National Revenue obsolescence the C.B.C. had a surplus of $6,500,000 for that year. That sum, we are told, is available now to be used in this program of capital expansion.
I am wondering what case is to be made out to support the necessity for a loan of $3 million in addition to the $6,250,000 from the grant and $15 million at the very least from the excise tax on receiving sets. Available in addition to those sums, let me remind you, are $6,500,000 of surplus from revenues in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954. What is the case the government proposes to make out for asking for a loan of $3 million in addition to these sums?

Mr. Chairman, we announced last year that the program would be for stations at Halifax, Vancouver, and Winnipeg, and a second station at Montreal, and one in Ottawa. We got funds then to the extent of $4,700,000, and this $3 million is to complete the program which was announced a year ago. The other money will be for programming and operations.

Are we to understand that this will complete the program? As I recall the figures, the program was going to involve an expenditure on capital account of $15 million to set up the system. It was approximately $15 million. The minister has referred to the figure of $4,700,000 laid out thus far, and $3 million by way of this loan. Are we to understand that with the assistance of this money, and $6,500,000 left over last year as surplus, that the $3 million will now secure the completion of that $15 million program of capital expansion to set up the television system across Canada?
What we contemplated two or three years ago.
This will complete it?
I think so, yes. iL'	'

My final question is this: How much time was allotted fo the communists. known as the Labouir-Progressive party, during the course of the last general election, as a share allotted to it of. the, time, made available to political parties during the campaign?
I am informed the answer to that was that it was two periods, and that was done by full agreement of the other political parties in the house.

Mr. Chairman, the minister talks about an agreement. I think he had better put his answer on the basis of a regulation. I wish to raise the question of the C.B.C. regulation which exists by reason of the fact that it has the sanction of the

Supply-National Revenue government, and permits communists in this country, calling themselves the Labour-Progressive party, to obtain free time on the air, simply because they nominate a designated number of candidates.
We know that the nomination of candidates is simply a fiction. It is only a fiction designed to enable them to bring about technical compliance with this regulation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I ask the minister if he does not think it is about time that that regulation was revised. We know perfectly well in this country that communists will just put up enough candidates to comply with the number prescribed.
I think it shocks a lot of people in this country to think that free time is being made available to communists, whose loyalty is not to this country, and who are able to obtain that time under a regulation that exists, and in my opinion has existed far too long. It is only a technical compliance, a fictional compliance with the intent of the regulation and it should be changed.

It was not done by regulation. It was done by agreement of the political parties. And if you want to know who the representatives of your party were, they were Mr. Grattan O'Leary and Mr. "Dick" Bell.

Let me tell the minister-and let there be no misunderstanding about it- that we are dealing with a regulation. And we are dealing with a regulation that has existed for some considerable time. And those to whom the minister has made reference I have no doubt had no alternative but to accept this situation, in view of the existence of the regulation. To say that they accepted the principle of giving communists free time on the air is just to talk nonsense.
I tell the minister that what was done was done by reason of the existence of a regulation. It is not a new regulation; it has been there for some time and I submit it is high time some thought was given to it-a regulation that permits communists to have free time on the air at public expense.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I am most surprised to see the hon. member for Eglinton taking exception to the understanding about radio time. Having been in the Ontario house for many years, I would say that it ill becomes the opposition to blame


the C.B.C. for the time they have given the Labour-Progressive party. For I sat in the house in Ontario while the Leader of the Opposition in this house was the premier of Ontario. And he could have, in his own province, outlawed the communists and prevented them from sitting in the Ontario house, just as the premier of Quebec did, if he was sincere in his talking.

On a question of privilege; the hon. member has cast doubt, as he has plainly said, upon the sincerity of an hon. member in this house, namely the Leader of the Opposition. That is in my opinion against the rules of the house, and I hope he will be made to withdraw.
He was talking about the premier of Ontario.
He was talking about an hon. member in this house, and he questioned the sincerity of that hon. member. I suggest that language like that cannot be used in this house.
Mr. Chairman-

Just a word before we close this part of the discussion. I think we should be more clear on one point. My understanding is that, provided they can meet certain requirements, the recognized political parties in this country are entitled to free time on the air, from the broadcasting corporation. And that applies not only in national radio but, in my province at least, to the private stations. Because they give a certain amount of free time, too.
The Labour-Progressive party, or the communist party, if you wish to call it that-and I quite agree that it is the proper term-get their share of the free time as well. It is not necessary for me to come to the defence of the government in this matter; but the circumstances are there. And unless and until that party is declared an illegal political party in Canada it is entitled to the same rights and privileges as every other party.

I have a question to ask in regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Bow River about colour television. I am not quite satisfied with the explanation that was given. About three or four years ago an invention on colour television was announced. It was taken up by two different companies. One had to do with a scanning plate and the other a cylinder. It was said at that time that the cost of purchasing this gadget for making colour television was so small that anyone could procure it and it could be attached to any television set as you would an adapter. Immediately after that it was announced that the invention had been purchased by the television industry and that they were developing it. For two or three years nothing more was heard about it until a question came up in the United States senate or congress asking what had become of the invention and they set up a committee to see what was the delay in placing it on the market. The idea they advanced was that the public would be exploited in regard to the cost of the invention. I do not think the explanation given to the committee by the minister sufficiently covered the question raised by the hon. member for Bow River, that the public of Canada were not going to be exploited when colour television was perfected. Our own technical men, or a committee, should be set up to investigate and see that exploitation does not take place. Colour television sets are going to be in demand and the suggested cost is away out of line. Therefore this is an important matter. We should see that no exploitation of the Canadian public will take place.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on resolutions 53 and 54, having to do with the international shortwave broadcasting service, I wish to make a short statement in which I think will be incorporated the answers to the questions put by the hon. member for Lethbridge. I understand that the matter of the C.B.C. international service was discussed within the last day or two by the committee on external affairs, so that I assume that a great many of the points which might be brought out at this time have already been dealt with. However, may I say that the shortwave broadcasting service broadcasts regularly to Europe, Latin America and Australasia, as well as providing Canadian news and radio entertainment for the Canadian armed forces establishments in northern Canada and overseas in Korea and Europe. It is currently transmitting in 16 languages, for a total of some 115 hours a week, as well as having a regular relay service in Austria and Greece.
During July of 1953 a new service was inaugurated to eastern Europe, with the establishment of daily broadcasts in Polish. The international service is now therefore broadcasting regularly to three areas of eastern Europe in Czech and Slovak to Czechoslovakia, in Russian and Ukrainian to the U.S.S.R., and in Polish to Poland. In this way Canada is playing its part in the common western cause of seeking to bring the

truth to the peoples behind the iron curtain. In this area, the shortwave service works quite closely with the B.B.C. and the "Voice of America" in arranging its program schedules and facilities for the maximum effectiveness in combating jamming, and reaching the audience.
Languages of transmissions are English, French, Dutch, Norwegian, Danish, Swedish, Finnish, Italian, German, Czech, Slovak, Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Spanish, Portuguese.
The service broadcasts about seven hours a week to each of the countries behind the iron curtain. The general purposes of shortwave broadcasting from Canada are: 1. To secure general political and social good will and understanding for Canada in European, Latin American and commonwealth countries. 2. To project abroad Canada's aims and policies and the life and culture of our people. 3. To provide a reliable source of international and Canadian news for the peoples of eastern Europe; to counteract communist propaganda about the western world; through news, factual information and vigorous statement of our views on current topics to encourage the Soviet people to question their governmental policies and to oppose its aggressive tactics, and in the satellite countries to keep alive their contact with western democratic life and seek to frustrate the efforts of Soviet domination. 4. To provide an appropriate climate for diplomatic and trade relations with other countries and to promote the general activities of government departments in their work abroad.
As all members are aware, the implementation of these policies is carried on in close collaboration with the Department of External Affairs. That department has a special section whose function it is to provide political guidance on international issues and check on such scripts as are broadcast. This section has been in existence now for over a year and has proved its value as a day to day continuing link. Careful supervision is also exercised over all material before broadcast through a central policy control unit in the shortwave service. This unit checks on all news bulletins and political material and also prepares basic scripts for the use of various language services.
Regarding the audience behind the iron curtain, it is of course most difficult to assess how large a percentage of people are actually listening. We know that in Czechoslovakia until the time of the communist coup in February 1948 we had a large and steadily increasing audience. Reports from refugees and other sources would confirm us in believing that this large audience has continued to increase rather than decline. Similar sources

confirm that western broadcasts to the Soviet union are heard, particularly outside the Moscow area where such broadcasts are heavily jammed. In broadcasts to this area, Canada of course works closely with the major broadcasting organizations, the B.B.C. and the "Voice of America", to make jamming of western transmissions as difficult as possible and to ensure that as much of western broadcasts as possible reaches the audience.
The Department of External Affairs is also responsible for advising the international service on the initiation and development of program service to individual countries.
In the estimates for the year 1954-55 the increase of some 8 per cent is almost entirely due to higher operating costs resulting from union agreements negotiated or in process of negotiation with the corporation. With the addition of the Polish service in July 1953, no expansion of service has been made or is contemplated.

speechtext: It is time someone took himself seriously when the gentlemen who are here are here. We have to have more than merely "bringing the matter before people". This will not get results. I am not in favour of allowing this item to pass until the minister does give the commitment to me.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: There is an easy way to get the estimates through.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext:
I should like the minister to state whether it is not the case, as I have been given to understand, that copies of these
Supply-National Revenue international service broadcasts are now available to the members of this house upon request.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: That is an entirely different thing. The only way I have of knowing something about a broadcast is for somebody to tell me; that is the only way I have. I want to have the privilege of thumbing through the script of any broadcast that goes over our international service, and for which we are now voting appropriations of a considerable size. We are voting considerable sums of money, and I want to have that privilege, without somebody coming to me and-

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: Did you ever try writing to the C.B.C. to ask for a copy?

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: Yes, if I wrote to the C.B.C. for a copy they would willingly give it.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: They are all available and on file at Montreal.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: Am I to write and ask for any copies-

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: It does not cost you anything for postage.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend was more intelligent than that. Of course, I could get copies. They have always been willing to give them to me whenever I have asked for them. The only way I have of knowing whether or not a thing is acceptable to me, at least, is for somebody to listen to it. Well, I do not listen to the international service at all, but I want to have the privilege of being able to read anything that goes over the air. I want to find out what is going on, and that is all I am asking.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: I feel the hon. member's request is a reasonable one. I believe that for the sake of public relations it should be a very easy matter to have copies come to the parliamentary library. I do not believe there is anything of which the C.B.C. could not be proud. I believe that to avoid criticism of this sort copies might be made available to the parliamentary library and we would not hear anything more about it.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: Nobody would ever look at them.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: The Secretary of State says nobody would look at them, and perhaps that is so. Here , you have the simple fact that the minister does not want to say yes, and if anyone were to psychoanalyse that statement they would say there was something he wanted to hide.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext:
It is not a question of wanting to say yes. The money is not available

Supply
for it. It would require a lot of time and some staff. If the hon. member wants any particular script they are all on file in Montreal. All you have to do is make a request for it and you would have it in twenty-four hours.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: That is not good enough.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: We won't read them for you.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: It is not going to take a big staff to do this. There is one copy that is ready every time it is read over the air. All that we want is to have it translated into English and French and filed here.

maintopic: CKLW-TV CKSO-TV CFPA-TV CFQC-TV CKCK-TV CHCT-TV CFRN-TV
speechtext: The next thing you will want is a record.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
